title: CCPA: personal information in AI systems
trigger_rule: ca_users AND ccpa_business AND non_hipaa_personal_info AND (genai OR trains_genai_model OR predictive_ml)
triggers: A CCPA business uses AI models that can output personal information.
example_tools: LLM or foundation model trained on patient or member records that can reproduce personal details; chatbot fine-tuned on customer or patient conversations; AI model trained on claims or EHR data; vendor model that embeds individuals' data in its weights; analytics model used by a digital health company
exclusions: Not a freestanding AI rule: it only changes the CCPA definition of personal information, so it matters only to a 'business' that meets the CCPA thresholds (Civ. Code 1798.140(d)). CCPA carve-outs still apply, including medical information governed by the CMIA, PHI held by HIPAA covered entities and business associates, and CMIA providers/HIPAA covered entities treating patient information the same way (1798.145(c), 1798.146). Personal information does not include deidentified or aggregate consumer information (1798.140). Applies only to AI systems 'capable of outputting personal information'.
key_definitions: 'personal information' may exist in formats including 'physical formats' (paper, printed images, vinyl records, video tapes), 'digital formats' (text, image, audio, video files), and 'abstract digital formats, including compressed or encrypted files, metadata, or artificial intelligence systems that are capable of outputting personal information' (Civ. Code 1798.140(v)(3)); 'business' = for-profit entity doing business in California that meets one of three thresholds: annual gross revenue above $26,625,000 (CPI-adjusted from $25M, effective 2025-01-01), buys/sells/shares personal information of 100,000+ consumers or households, or derives 50%+ of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information (1798.140(d)); 'consumer' = a natural person who is a California resident (1798.140(i))
key_questions: Is the company a for-profit business over the CCPA thresholds (revenue above $26.6M, 100,000+ consumers or households, or 50%+ of revenue from selling/sharing data)?; Does the AI model memorize or reproduce individuals' personal information in its outputs?; Was the model trained on California residents' data?; Is the underlying data CMIA medical information or HIPAA PHI (exempt from CCPA) or non-HIPAA consumer health data (covered)?; Can you honor deletion and access requests that reach the model and its training data?
obligations: Personal information can exist in physical, digital, and abstract digital formats, including AI systems capable of outputting personal information, so CCPA consumer rights and business duties apply to personal information in those forms.
enforcement: CPPA and AG under CCPA.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 802, Stats. 2024; approved by Governor 2024-09-28. Row was from researcher memory; existence, date, and content now confirmed. Same definition carried in SB 1223 SEC. 1.5.

title: Automated Decisions Safety Act
trigger_rule: ca_users AND (automated_significant_decision OR automation_bias_risk) AND (cdss OR utilization_review OR workforce_decisions)
triggers: Would apply to a developer or deployer of an automated decision system that takes a person's data and issues a score, classification, or recommendation used to make or facilitate a consequential decision, including health care or health insurance decisions; HIPAA covered entities and business associates and FDA-regulated medical devices are largely excluded.
example_tools: AI prior-authorization or claims-denial scoring tool; patient risk-stratification model used to allocate care management or access; automated eligibility or financial-assistance screening for health coverage; AI hiring or scheduling screening tool used by a health system; benefits-eligibility determination engine
exclusions: Not law (died on the Senate floor; no vote before the 2026-08-31 deadline); signal only. If it had passed (2026-08-28 amended text): excluded HIPAA covered entities and their business associates (22756.5(d)(1)), except for employment decisions, patient financial-assistance eligibility, and the pre-decision notice in 22756.2(a); excluded FDA-regulated medical devices and combination products and FDA-overseen R&D (22756.5(e), (g)); excluded CLIA laboratory-test support ADS (22756.5(h)); excluded drug and device manufacturing/quality GxP ADS (22756.5(i)); excluded cybersecurity, fraud, physical security, advertisements, spam/robocall filtering, aircraft, and national security systems (22756.5(a), (j)); GenAI not intended or advertised for profiling a person to make or facilitate a consequential decision is not a 'covered ADS' (22756(e)(2)); correction and appeal duties only for deployers with more than 25 employees (22756.2(c)); GLBA-regulated developers and deployers excused for financial-services decisions.
key_definitions: 'automated decision system' = computational process from machine learning, statistical modeling, data analytics, or AI that issues simplified output (score, classification, recommendation) designed or used to assist or replace human discretionary decisionmaking and materially impacts natural persons; excludes spam filters, firewalls, antivirus, identity verification/access tools, calculators, databases, datasets, spreadsheets (B&P 22756(c)); 'consequential decision' = a decision materially affecting the cost, terms, quality, or accessibility of employment, education, housing, health care and health insurance (including mental health, dental, vision), financial services, government benefits, or insurance (22756(d)); 'covered ADS' = an ADS designed for or used by a deployer to profile a natural person to make or facilitate a consequential decision (22756(e)); 'profile' = use a covered ADS that takes the subject's personal information as input and issues a score, classification, or recommendation to evaluate the subject or predict outcomes (22756(r)); 'deployer' = a person or agency that uses a covered ADS to make or facilitate a consequential decision, directly or through a third party (22756(g)); 'developer' = one that designs, codes, substantially modifies, or produces an ADS that makes or facilitates a consequential decision (22756(h)); 'adverse outcome' = denial, termination, revocation, or material reduction or restriction of access, eligibility, or service (22756(a))
key_questions: Is this tool an ADS that takes a person's data and produces a score, classification, or recommendation used to assist or replace a human decision?; Does it make or facilitate a decision about health care access, health insurance, employment, or benefits?; Are you a HIPAA covered entity or business associate (largely exempt except for employment and financial-assistance decisions)?; Is the product an FDA-regulated medical device?; Are you a developer, a deployer, or both; does a deployer use it for more than 6,000 people in three years?; Does the deployer have more than 25 employees (correction and appeal duties)?
obligations: Would require developers to give deployers instructions for each developer-approved use, fine-tuning information, and the technical information needed to comply, and to keep that documentation for the product's life plus five years. Would require deployers to give a plain-language notice before finalizing a consequential decision (including health care and health insurance) made or facilitated by a covered automated decision system, and after an adverse outcome a description of the system's role and a process to request the data and parameters used; deployers with more than 25 employees would also have to allow correction of personal information and an appeal, on 30-day or 30-business-day timelines; deployers must keep records for five years and limit data use to what is reasonably necessary and proportionate. The 2026-08-28 amended text contains no impact-testing duty.
enforcement: Would be enforced by the Attorney General (civil penalty up to $25,000 per violation, injunctive and declaratory relief, fees), with a 60-day cure notice that expires 2030-01-01. The mirror text shows deleted and added language merged, so whether district attorneys, city attorneys, the Civil Rights Department, or the Labor Commissioner kept standing is not confirmed.
notes: Digital Democracy history (Tier 2): passed Assembly 2025-06-02; two-year bill on Senate inactive file from 2025-09-13; revived and amended 2026-08-21/08-28; last action 2026-08-30 "Read second time. Ordered to third reading." No Senate floor vote before the 2026-08-31 deadline to pass bills, and not in the Governor's signed or vetoed lists. Marked died by inference from that deadline; the session formally ends 2026-11-30. Obligations summarized from the 2026-08-28 amended text.

title: LEAD for Kids Act (companion chatbots and children)
triggers: Would have applied to operators of companion chatbots available to children.
example_tools: AI companion app available to teens; character chatbot platform open to under-18 users; AI friend or confidant bot that remembers past chats; emotional-support or anxiety chatbot a child can download; AI therapy-style chatbot marketed to adolescents
exclusions: Not law (vetoed 2025-10-13); signal only. If it had been signed: 'companion chatbot' excluded systems used by a business solely for customer service or information about its products/services, systems designed and marketed solely for efficiency, research, or technical assistance, and systems used solely for internal or employee-productivity purposes (B&P 22757.21(c)(2)); a user was not a 'child' if, before 2027-01-01, the operator lacked actual knowledge the user is a child, and from 2027-01-01 if the operator reasonably determined the user is not a child (22757.22(b)); 'child' limited to California residents under 18 (22757.21(b)). Superseded in substance by SB 243 and SB 1119 (Adam's Law).
key_definitions: 'companion chatbot' = a generative AI system with a natural language interface that simulates a sustained humanlike relationship by (A) retaining prior interactions and preferences to personalize and sustain engagement, (B) asking unprompted emotion-based questions beyond a direct response, and (C) sustaining ongoing dialogue on matters personal to the user (22757.21(c)(1)); 'child' = a natural person under 18 who resides in California (22757.21(b)); 'operator' = a person, entity, or state/local agency that makes a companion chatbot available to users (22757.21(e))
key_questions: Does the bot retain prior sessions and preferences, ask unprompted emotion-based questions, and sustain personal dialogue (all three)?; Is it used only for customer service, internal productivity, or technical assistance?; Can California users under 18 access it, and what do you know or reasonably determine about their age?; Could the bot offer mental health therapy without licensed supervision or encourage self-harm, disordered eating, or drug use?
obligations: Would have barred operators from making companion chatbots available to children unless not foreseeably capable of specified harms, including encouraging self-harm or offering mental health therapy without professional supervision.
enforcement: Not applicable.
notes: Veto 2025-10-13 confirmed in gov.ca.gov 10.13.25 legislative update (veto list) and DD history (veto consideration stricken 2026-01-22). Enrolled text via Digital Democracy (Tier 2).

title: CCPA: ban on sale/sharing of sensitive personal information
trigger_rule: ca_users AND ccpa_business AND shares_personal_data AND non_hipaa_personal_info
triggers: Would have applied to businesses selling or sharing CCPA sensitive personal information, which includes health data.
example_tools: wellness or fitness app that shares health data with advertisers; digital health app that sells user health information to data brokers; consumer symptom checker with ad-tech trackers; connected-device or wearable company licensing health data to third parties; mental health app with analytics SDKs that send sensitive data to third parties
exclusions: Not law (vetoed 2026-09-27); signal only. If it had been signed, the ban on selling or sharing sensitive personal information (1798.121(e)(1)) was subject to the existing carve-outs in 1798.140(ad)(2)(A) and (ah)(2)(A), and a commercial credit reporting agency could sell a Social Security number solely to identify a consumer's relationship to a business the consumer owns (1798.121(e)(2)). Only CCPA 'businesses' were reached, and medical information under the CMIA and PHI under HIPAA remain outside the CCPA (1798.145(c)).
key_definitions: 'sensitive personal information' includes personal information collected and analyzed concerning a consumer's health, plus genetic, neural, biometric-for-identification, precise geolocation, and similar categories (Civ. Code 1798.140(ae)); 'sell' = selling, renting, releasing, disclosing, or otherwise communicating a consumer's personal information to a third party for monetary or other valuable consideration (1798.140(ad)); 'share' = communicating personal information to a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising (1798.140(ah)); 'business' = see CA-CCPA thresholds (1798.140(d))
key_questions: Is the company a CCPA 'business' (revenue above $26.6M, 100,000+ consumers or households, or 50%+ of revenue from selling/sharing)?; Does the product collect health information that is not CMIA medical information or HIPAA PHI?; Is any of it sold to or shared with third parties, including ad-tech or analytics partners, for advertising or value?; Does a service-provider or contractor arrangement apply to the recipient?
obligations: Would have barred businesses, service providers, and contractors from selling or sharing sensitive personal information to third parties, with narrow exceptions.
enforcement: Not applicable.
notes: Veto 2026-09-27 confirmed in Digital Democracy history (Tier 2); gov.ca.gov veto list not checked. Signal, tagged E on health-data grounds; borderline.

title: Customer service chatbots
effective_date_notes: No operative-date clause; default 2027-01-01 (text references platforms in use as of 2027-01-01).
triggers: A business with more than $500M in national gross annual revenue uses a customer service chatbot with California customers (health plans and large vendors may qualify). Hospitals are exempt for communications relating to health care services, including scheduling, billing, utilization management, and prior authorization.
example_tools: health plan member-services chatbot; AI phone agent for a pharmacy chain or PBM; digital health company's customer support bot for billing and subscriptions; health insurer's virtual assistant for claims questions; large medical device or supplies retailer's support chatbot
exclusions: Applies only to a 'large private business' (over $500M national gross annual revenue) (22625(g)); does not apply to a hospital when its communications relate to provision, coordination, management, administration, payment, or operation of health care services, including patient care, scheduling, intake, referrals, care coordination, utilization management, prior authorization, discharge planning, billing, and insurance (22628(g)(3)); excludes exclusive business lines (employee-only or business-to-business) (22628(g)(2)), PUC-regulated telecom and water services under GO 133/103-A with any corrective plan (22628(g)(1)), and consumer reporting agencies (22628(g)(4)); 'services' excludes free tiers (22625(j)); the 15-minute response does not apply to email, web forms, or voicemail, and businesses need not add channels not offered as of 2027-01-01 (22627(e)); inability due to unforeseen circumstances or emergencies is not a violation (22628(f)); no private right of action (22628(d)).
key_definitions: 'customer service chatbot' = an AI system with a natural language interface providing adaptive, human-like responses used for direct customer service or support relating to the sale or delivery of goods or services (B&P 22625(d)); 'large private business' = a business with more than $500,000,000 in national gross annual revenue that provides goods and services to customers (22625(g)); 'customer' = a natural person residing in California, by account address (22625(b)); 'hospital' = health facility licensed under H&S 1250(a), (b), or (f) (22625(f)); 'services' = services for which the customer pays, excluding free options (22625(j)); 'exclusive business lines' = channels intended solely for employees or business-to-business communications (22625(e))
key_questions: Does the company have more than $500M in national gross annual revenue?; Is the company a licensed hospital, and does the chatbot handle health care-related communications?; Does the chatbot serve California-resident consumers (vs. businesses or employees only)?; Does it handle customer service or support for paid goods or services?; Which channels (chat, phone) does the company already offer for customer service?
obligations: Do not represent a customer service chatbot as human; give a clear disclosure where a reasonable person could be misled; during regular business hours provide a simple way to request a human agent and make a good-faith effort to connect within 15 minutes or schedule a callback within one business day; keep holds under 15 minutes and cumulative waits under one hour; online businesses with phone service must post the number.
enforcement: Public prosecutors only; civil penalty up to $5,000 for an initial violation and $10,000 per subsequent violation; no private right of action.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 733, Stats. 2026; approved by Governor 2026-09-28 (gov.ca.gov 9/28/2026 release). Hospital exemption (22628(g)(3)) limits health relevance to plans, non-hospital providers, and vendors. Typo fixed: "Staus Firm" was The Strauss Firm (no longer relied on).

title: Health care services: artificial intelligence (clinical judgment; consumer health chatbots under CMIA)
effective_date_notes: No operative-date clause in chaptered text; default 2027-01-01.
trigger_rule: ca_users AND (((org_provider OR org_developer) AND cdss) OR (genai AND chatbot AND patient_facing AND health_info))
triggers: A health facility, clinic, physician's office, or group practice uses AI, including a clinical decision support system, in patient care; or a business offers consumers a "health care chatbot" (generative AI with a natural-language interface marketed to support health services and using consumers' health information) for managing their information or for diagnosis, treatment, or management of a condition.
example_tools: sepsis or deterioration early-warning alert used by a hospital; AI differential-diagnosis or treatment-recommendation tool for physicians; AI triage nurse that directs medical assistants; consumer health chatbot that answers symptom questions using the user's health data; AI app that helps patients manage a chronic condition through a conversational assistant
exclusions: Facility/clinician rule (B&P 22758.5) does not apply to automated decision systems used for documentation and communication that do not involve professional judgment, e.g. automated messages telling patients their record was updated, reminders, or helping patients find information at their request (22758.5(d)); trainees using AI in a supervised course of study or training program toward licensure are not barred (22758.5(b)(2)); 'clinical decision support system' excludes appointment booking/canceling/rescheduling, appointment reminders, patient education and pre-visit materials, and payment processing, to the extent doing these does not require a license (22758.5(e)(4)); the facility rule reaches only health facilities, clinics, physician offices, and group-practice offices, not health plans or vendors directly. Chatbot rule (Civ. Code 56.06(f)) reaches only a generative AI system meeting all three prongs of 'health care chatbot' (adaptive human-like responses, marketed as supporting health services, uses consumer health information); a business deemed a provider under 56.06 is a provider only for the CMIA, not for other laws.
key_definitions: 'clinical decision support system' = an AI system producing a prediction, classification, recommendation, evaluation, or analysis that aids clinical decisionmaking on timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment; excludes appointment management, reminders, patient education/pre-visit materials, and payment processing where no license is required (B&P 22758.5(e)(4)); 'automated decision system' = computational process from ML, statistics, data analytics, or AI issuing simplified output (score, classification, recommendation) used to assist or replace human discretionary decisions that materially impacts people; excludes spam filters, firewalls, antivirus, identity/access tools, calculators, databases, datasets (22758.5(e)(2)); 'health care chatbot' = a generative AI system with a natural language interface that (1) provides adaptive, human-like responses, (2) is marketed as facilitating or supporting health services to a consumer, and (3) uses 'health care chatbot information' (physical or mental health or wellness information the consumer provides or allows access to, or that the chatbot collects, generates, or infers) to support health services (Civ. Code 56.05(i)); 'artificial intelligence' and 'generative artificial intelligence' as defined in H&S Code 1339.75 (22758.5(e)(1), (5); 56.05(a), (h)); 'office of a group practice' = two or more physicians organized as a partnership, professional corporation, or nonprofit corporation (H&S 1339.75)
key_questions: Is the user a licensed health facility, clinic, solo physician office, or group practice office (vs. a health plan, vendor, or consumer app)?; Does the tool produce a prediction, classification, recommendation, evaluation, or analysis that aids decisions on timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment?; Does the tool perform, or direct unlicensed staff to perform, a clinical function that legally requires a license?; Is the tool limited to documentation or communication that involves no professional judgment (reminders, record-update notices, information lookup)?; Is the tool only for scheduling, reminders, patient education, or payment processing?; Is it a generative AI chatbot marketed to consumers as supporting health services that uses their health or wellness information?; Is it offered so consumers can manage their information or for diagnosis, treatment, or management of a condition?
obligations: Facilities, clinics, and physician/group offices must take reasonable steps so licensed providers retain independent professional judgment when care is informed by clinical decision support output, and must not use AI to independently perform, or to direct/supervise unlicensed staff in, clinical functions that require a license (supervised trainees exempted; documentation and communications not involving professional judgment exempted). A business offering a health care chatbot is deemed a provider of health care under the CMIA and must meet CMIA confidentiality standards.
enforcement: Physicians: Medical Board or Osteopathic Medical Board; licensing boards may seek injunctions (B&P 125.5) where the violation is unlicensed practice; CMIA penalties and remedies apply to health care chatbot businesses.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 854, Stats. 2026; approved by Governor 2026-09-30 (also listed in gov.ca.gov 9.30.2026 AI release). No urgency or operative-date clause, so effective 2027-01-01. Citation corrected: the clinical-judgment rule is in the B&P Code, not the H&S Code.

title: Generative AI training data transparency
effective_date_notes: Statute effective 2025-01-01 (Stats. 2024). effective_date is the first posting deadline: documentation due on or before 2026-01-01, and before each later public release or substantial modification (Civ. Code 3111). Applies to systems released or substantially modified since 2022-01-01.
trigger_rule: ca_users AND (trains_genai_model OR (genai AND NOT third_party_model))
triggers: A developer makes a generative AI system or service available to Californians (including a health-focused generative tool), and has released or substantially modified it on or after 2022-01-01.
example_tools: public-facing medical LLM or health chatbot built on a fine-tuned model; generative AI clinical note or patient-letter writer sold to the public; AI medical image generator or synthetic-data tool offered to Californians; consumer symptom-advice assistant trained or fine-tuned on health data; generative model released on a public API
exclusions: No posting duty for a generative AI system whose sole purpose is security and integrity, whose sole purpose is operating aircraft in the national airspace, or that is developed for national security, military, or defense purposes and made available only to a federal entity (Civ. Code 3111(b)); 'members of the public' excludes affiliates and a hospital's medical staff members, so a system built only for affiliates or for a hospital's own medical staff is not 'for use by members of the public' (3110(b)); applies only to generative AI released or substantially modified on or after 2022-01-01 and made publicly available to Californians (3111); non-generative AI (e.g. a risk score) is outside it.
key_definitions: 'developer' = a person, partnership, state or local government agency, or corporation that designs, codes, produces, or substantially modifies an AI system or service for use by members of the public; members of the public excludes affiliates and a hospital's medical staff members (Civ. Code 3110(b)); 'generative artificial intelligence' = AI that can generate derived synthetic content, such as text, images, video, and audio, that emulates the structure and characteristics of its training data (3110(c)); 'substantially modifies' = new version, release, or update that materially changes functionality or performance, including retraining or fine-tuning (3110(d)); 'train' includes testing, validating, or fine-tuning by the developer (3110(f))
key_questions: Does the tool generate content (text, images, audio, video), i.e. is it generative AI?; Is it made publicly available to Californians, free or paid (vs. only to affiliates or a hospital's own medical staff)?; Was it released or substantially modified (including fine-tuning or retraining) on or after 2022-01-01?; Did you design, code, produce, fine-tune, or retrain it (vs. only use someone else's model unmodified)?; Is its sole purpose security/integrity, aircraft operation, or federal-only national security?
obligations: By 2026-01-01, and before each later public release or substantial modification of a generative AI system or service released since 2022-01-01, post documentation on the developer's website summarizing training datasets: sources/owners, purpose, size, data types, whether they include copyrighted material, personal information, or aggregate consumer information, whether licensed or purchased, cleaning/processing, collection period, first-use dates, and synthetic data use. Exempt: security/integrity-only systems, aircraft operation, and national-security systems available only to federal entities.
enforcement: No express penalty or enforcement provision in the text.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 817, Stats. 2024; approved by Governor 2024-09-28. Statute effective 2025-01-01; first posting deadline 2026-01-01 (used as effective_date). "Developer" excludes affiliates and a hospital's medical staff members from "members of the public". Litigation: xAI v. Bonta (C.D. Cal.) denied a preliminary injunction on 2026-03-04; appeal No. 26-1591 pending in the Ninth Circuit with no ruling found as of 2026-10-12 (secondary sources; docket not read). The law remains in effect.

title: Health care services: AI (clinical decision support; anti-retaliation for override)
citation: Not applicable (vetoed); would have added Civil Code 1714.48 and Labor Code 2820 et seq.
trigger_rule: ca_users AND cdss AND (org_provider OR org_developer)
triggers: Would have applied to providers using AI clinical decision support systems and protected workers who override AI outputs.
example_tools: sepsis or deterioration alert that nurses can override; AI radiology triage tool whose recommendation a physician may reject; EHR clinical recommendation engine; AI-driven care pathway or order-set suggestions; AI risk score used by care managers
exclusions: Not law (vetoed 2026-09-30); signal only. If it had been signed: the superseding-cause rule would not have limited other affirmative defenses, causation or foreseeability evidence, comparative fault evidence, or evidence of reasonable precautions such as clear disclosures to the health facility, clinic, physician's office, or group practice (Civ. Code 1714.48(c)); it would not have applied to a professional negligence action under Code Civ. Proc. 340.5 against a licensed or certified person providing direct patient care (1714.48(d)); 'clinical decision support system' excluded appointment management, reminders, patient education/pre-visit materials, and payment processing where no license is required (1714.48(a)(3)); the Labor Code anti-retaliation rule covered only workers providing direct patient care and did not relieve them of the standard of care, scope-of-practice limits, or employer written policies (Lab. Code 2821(b)(2)).
key_definitions: 'clinical decision support system' = an AI system that produces a prediction, classification, recommendation, evaluation, or analysis that aids clinical decisionmaking on timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment (Civ. Code 1714.48(a)(3); Lab. Code 2820(c)); 'automated decision system' = computational process from machine learning, statistics, data analytics, or AI issuing a score, classification, or recommendation used to assist or replace human discretionary decisions that materially impacts natural persons (1714.48(a)(2)); defendants covered = anyone who 'developed, modified, selected, or deployed' a CDS system (1714.48(b)); 'worker providing direct patient care' (Lab. Code 2821)
key_questions: Does the tool produce predictions, classifications, or recommendations that aid diagnosis, treatment, or timing of care?; Did you develop, modify, select, or deploy it?; Do employees get disciplined or penalized for overriding or following its output?; Does your policy require staff to accept or defer to the tool's output?
obligations: Would have barred defendants who developed or deployed a clinical decision support system from arguing that a worker's failure to override its output was a superseding cause, and barred employers from retaliating against direct-care workers for overriding or relying on CDS output, enforced by the Labor Commissioner.
enforcement: Would have been enforced via Labor Commissioner.
notes: Veto 2026-09-30 confirmed in gov.ca.gov 9.30.2026 legislative update (veto list, with veto message link) and DD history; the "signed" reading in one researcher fetch was wrong. Enrolled text read via Digital Democracy (Tier 2). Veto message not read.

title: Health care services: generative AI patient communications
trigger_rule: ca_users AND (org_provider OR org_developer) AND genai AND patient_comm AND clinical_info_comm AND NOT clinician_review
triggers: A health facility, clinic, physician's office, or group practice uses generative AI to produce written or spoken patient communications about patient clinical information (not administrative matters such as scheduling or billing).
example_tools: generative AI drafts of patient portal replies about test results; AI-generated after-visit summaries or discharge instructions sent to patients; LLM chat-based telehealth assistant answering clinical questions; AI voice agent that calls patients about lab results or medication changes; AI-drafted patient letters explaining a diagnosis
exclusions: Does not apply when the AI-generated communication is read and reviewed by a human licensed or certified health care provider before it goes out (1339.75(b)); does not apply to administrative matters such as appointment scheduling, billing, or other clerical or business matters, which are outside 'patient clinical information' (1339.75(c)(7)); applies only to health facilities, clinics, solo physician offices, and group practice offices, not to health plans, vendors, or consumer apps; does not apply to non-generative AI.
key_definitions: 'generative artificial intelligence' = AI that can generate derived synthetic content, including images, videos, audio, text, and other digital content (H&S 1339.75(c)(3)); 'patient clinical information' = information relating to the health status of a patient; excludes appointment scheduling, billing, and other clerical or business matters (1339.75(c)(7)); 'physician's office' = office of a physician in solo practice (1339.75(c)(8)); 'office of a group practice' = office(s) where two or more physicians are organized as a partnership, professional corporation, or nonprofit corporation (1339.75(c)(6)); 'health facility' per H&S 1250 and 'clinic' per H&S 1200 (1339.75(c)(2), (5)); 'health care provider' = person licensed or certified under B&P Division 2 (1339.75(c)(4))
key_questions: Is the sender a licensed health facility, clinic, physician office, or group practice?; Does the tool use generative AI to write or speak the message?; Is the message about the patient's health status (vs. scheduling, billing, or other administrative matters)?; Does a licensed or certified provider read and review each message before it is sent?; What channel is used (letter/email, continuous chat, audio, video), since disclaimer placement differs?
obligations: Generative-AI patient communications about patient clinical information must include (1) a disclaimer that the message was AI-generated (start of letters/emails; displayed throughout chat and video; spoken at start and end of audio) and (2) clear instructions for reaching a human provider or other appropriate person. Communications read and reviewed by a licensed or certified human provider are exempt.
enforcement: Licensed health facilities: H&S Code Art. 3 (commencing 1275) licensing enforcement; licensed clinics: Art. 3 (commencing 1225); physicians: Medical Board or Osteopathic Medical Board.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 848, Stats. 2024; approved by Governor 2024-09-28 (also gov.ca.gov 9.28.24 update). No operative-date clause, so default 2025-01-01. Administrative matters (scheduling, billing) are outside "patient clinical information".

title: Artificial intelligence: defense that AI autonomously caused harm barred
triggers: A defendant who developed, modified, or used AI is sued for harm caused to a plaintiff.
example_tools: any clinical AI tool (diagnostic algorithm, CDS alert, triage bot) involved in a malpractice or injury claim; autonomous AI prior-auth or care-management agent alleged to have caused harm; AI symptom checker whose advice is alleged to have injured a user; ambient scribe that inserted an error into the record
exclusions: Does not bar other affirmative defenses, including evidence relevant to causation or foreseeability, or evidence of the comparative fault of any other person or entity (Civ. Code 1714.46(c)); applies only in actions against a defendant who developed, modified, or used the AI alleged to have caused the harm (1714.46(b)).
key_definitions: 'artificial intelligence' = an engineered or machine-based system that varies in its level of autonomy and that can, for explicit or implicit objectives, infer from the input it receives how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments (Civ. Code 1714.46(a))
key_questions: Did your company develop, modify, or use the AI tool?; Could the tool's output plausibly cause physical, financial, or other harm to a patient or user?; Would your defense rely on the AI having acted autonomously?
obligations: A defendant who developed, modified, or used AI may not assert as a defense that the AI autonomously caused the plaintiff's harm; other affirmative defenses and comparative-fault evidence remain available.
enforcement: Private civil litigation.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 672, Stats. 2025; approved by Governor 2025-10-13 (also gov.ca.gov 10/13/2025 release). Included under criterion B (liability for any AI tool including clinical).

title: Health care professions: deceptive terms or letters: artificial intelligence
triggers: A developer or deployer of an AI or GenAI system, program, or device uses a term, letter, or phrase in its advertising or functionality that indicates or implies the care, advice, reports, or assessments are being provided by a licensed health care professional (for example a chatbot calling itself a doctor or nurse).
example_tools: symptom checker that presents itself as 'Dr. AI' or 'your AI nurse'; AI therapy chatbot marketed as a 'therapist' or 'counselor'; virtual nutritionist or dietitian bot; AI app whose reports are labeled 'physician-reviewed' without a physician; health chatbot that signs messages with 'RN' or 'MD'
exclusions: None stated in the text as express exemptions. In practice it reaches only uses of terms, letters, or phrases that indicate or imply that the care, advice, reports, or assessments come from a natural person holding the relevant health care license (4999.9(b), (c)); AI that does not use protected titles or imply licensed human care is outside it.
key_definitions: 'health care profession' = any profession licensed or regulated under B&P Division 2 or an initiative act referred to in it (B&P 4999.8(c)); 'artificial intelligence' per Gov. Code 11546.45.5 (4999.8(a)); 'generative artificial intelligence' per Gov. Code 11549.64 (4999.8(b))
key_questions: Does the product name, persona, marketing, or interface use a licensed title or letters (doctor, Dr., MD, nurse, RN, therapist, pharmacist, etc.)?; Do the wording or design imply that advice, reports, or assessments come from a licensed human professional?; Do you develop or deploy the AI system (vs. merely host it)?; Is a licensed professional actually providing or reviewing the care?
obligations: Do not use terms, letters, or phrases in an AI product's advertising or functionality that indicate or imply the advice or care comes from a natural person holding the relevant health care license; existing title-protection provisions of the B&P Code are enforceable against those who develop or deploy such AI systems. Each prohibited use is a separate violation.
enforcement: Jurisdiction of the appropriate health care professional licensing board or enforcement agency; boards may seek injunctions or restraining orders under B&P 125.5. Each use is a separate violation.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 615, Stats. 2025; approved by Governor 2025-10-11 (also gov.ca.gov 10.11.25 update). Default effective 2026-01-01. Researcher's "design elements" wording is not in the text; removed.

title: California AI Transparency Act amendments (delay and platform/device provenance)
effective_date_notes: Statute effective 2026-01-01 (its delay of SB 942 to 2026-08-02 took effect then). Its own new duties start later: large online platforms and GenAI hosting platforms 2027-01-01; capture-device makers 2028-01-01 for devices first sold on or after that date. AB 2713 (2026, Ch. 856) revised 22757.3.1 platform duties, still operative 2027-01-01.
triggers: A large online platform (public social media, file-sharing, mass messaging, or search service with more than 2 million unique monthly users) distributes content; a GenAI hosting platform offers generative model weights or source code for download by Californians; or a manufacturer sells cameras, phones, or voice recorders in California first produced on or after 2028-01-01. Generative AI providers' own disclosure duties are under SB 942 as amended.
example_tools: health social network or patient community platform with over 2 million monthly users; open-model hub hosting downloadable generative model weights; smartphone or camera maker selling devices in California; voice recorder or dictation device manufacturer; large telehealth or health-content video platform
exclusions: 'Large online platform' covers only public-facing social media, file-sharing, mass messaging (over 100 recipients at once), or stand-alone search platforms with more than 2,000,000 unique monthly users in the prior 12 months, and excludes broadband internet access and telecommunications services (B&P 22757.1(h)); capture-device duties apply only to devices first produced for sale in California on or after 2028-01-01, only to the extent technically feasible and standards-compliant, and not to persons exclusively assembling devices (22757.3.3, 22757.1(c)(2)); platforms must avoid stripping provenance data only to the extent technically feasible (22757.3.1(b)); hosting platforms are liable only for knowingly offering non-compliant systems (22757.3.2); non-user-generated video games excluded (22757.5).
key_definitions: 'large online platform' = public-facing social media, file-sharing, mass messaging platform, or stand-alone search engine distributing content to users who did not create it, with more than 2,000,000 unique monthly users in the preceding 12 months; excludes broadband and telecom services (B&P 22757.1(h)); 'GenAI hosting platform' = website or app that makes source code or model weights of a GenAI system available for download by a California resident (22757.1(g)); 'capture device' = device that can record photos, audio, or video, including cameras, phones with cameras or microphones, and voice recorders (22757.1(b)); 'capture device manufacturer' = person producing a capture device for sale in the state, excluding assembly-only (22757.1(c)); 'provenance data' and 'system provenance data' (22757.1(o), (p))
key_questions: Is your service a large online platform (social media, file-sharing, mass messaging, or search distributing others' content, with more than 2,000,000 unique monthly users), a GenAI system hosting platform, or a capture-device maker? (The 2,000,000-user threshold is in the large online platform definition only.); Do you run a public-facing social, file-sharing, mass messaging, or search platform with more than 2 million unique monthly users?; Do you host downloadable model weights or source code for generative AI?; Do you manufacture cameras, phones, or recorders sold in California, first produced on or after 2028-01-01?; Do you strip metadata or provenance data from uploaded content?
obligations: Large online platforms (>2M monthly users) must detect standards-compliant provenance data, show users whether provenance data exists, let users inspect it, and not knowingly strip it; GenAI hosting platforms must not knowingly offer GenAI systems that do not place required disclosures; capture-device makers must offer latent disclosures and embed them by default.
enforcement: See SB 942.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history); statute dates also confirmed in LegiScan text. Ch. 674, Stats. 2025; approved by Governor 2025-10-13. Edge case: indirect health relevance. The bill took effect 2026-01-01 (delaying SB 942's operative date to 2026-08-02); effective_date is set to its first new duty (2027-01-01) per the schema's convention for amending statutes.

title: Attorney General legal advisory: application of California law to AI in healthcare
citation: Cal. Atty. Gen. Legal Advisory, "Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare" (Jan. 13, 2025)
triggers: A healthcare provider, insurer, vendor, developer, or investor develops, sells, or uses AI in health care in California.
example_tools: AI claims-denial or utilization review tool; generative AI that drafts clinical notes or patient messages; risk-prediction model that decides who gets care management or appointments; AI scheduling tool that double-books predicted no-shows; health data platform that trains models on patient records
exclusions: Non-binding guidance, not a statute or regulation; it creates no new duties and says it does not address all laws or avenues of enforcement. It does not cover federal requirements (FDA software-as-a-medical-device rules, FTC Act, HHS Section 1557 and ONC rules, CMS guidance), which it names as outside its scope. Underlying laws carry their own exemptions (for example CMIA/HIPAA, Knox-Keene scope).
key_definitions: 'artificial intelligence' for the advisory = a machine-based system that can, for human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments (15 U.S.C. 9401(3)); the advisory also cites California's definition (Gov. Code 11546.45.5): an engineered or machine-based system that varies in autonomy and infers from input how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments; 'automated decision systems' = a computational process from machine learning, statistical modeling, data analytics, or AI that issues simplified output (score, classification, recommendation) used to assist or replace human discretionary decisionmaking and materially impacts natural persons (Gov. Code 11546.45.5(a)(2)); audience = 'healthcare providers, insurers, vendors, investors, and other healthcare entities that develop, sell, and use' AI
key_questions: Are you a provider, insurer, vendor, developer, or investor that develops, sells, or uses AI in healthcare in California?; Does the tool influence diagnosis, treatment, coverage, scheduling, or billing?; Could its output override a clinician's view of medical necessity or disadvantage groups with limited past access?; Do you test, validate, and audit it for bias, and tell patients how their data trains AI?; Does the AI practice medicine or make treatment decisions in place of licensed professionals?
obligations: Non-binding advisory: existing consumer protection (UCL), civil rights, competition, and patient privacy laws (CMIA and others) apply to healthcare AI; developers, providers, insurers, and vendors should test, validate, and audit AI systems, avoid discriminatory or harmful uses, and be transparent with patients about AI use and use of their data for training.
enforcement: AG enforcement of underlying laws (UCL, Unruh, CMIA, etc.).
notes: Tier 1: oag.ca.gov press release (2025-01-13) and advisory PDF. Missing citation filled in. Included as interpretive guidance (criterion D applied by analogy; D lists federal instruments). The companion general AI advisory (same date) has no row.

title: California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by CPRA
effective_date_notes: Operative 2020-01-01 (Civ. Code 1798.198). CPRA amendments operative 2023-01-01; civil and administrative enforcement of CPRA-added provisions from 2023-07-01 (1798.185(d)). CPPA ADMT/risk/cyber regulations effective 2026-01-01 (separate row).
triggers: A for-profit business doing business in California with annual gross revenue above $26,625,000, or that buys, sells, or shares the personal information of 100,000+ California consumers or households a year, or that earns 50%+ of revenue from selling or sharing personal information, handles California residents' personal information, including health information that is not covered by the HIPAA or CMIA exemptions.
example_tools: direct-to-consumer health app or symptom checker not run by a HIPAA covered entity; wellness, fitness, or mental-wellness app and wearable data platform; consumer-facing health chatbot; AI model trained on consumer data; neurotech or sleep-tracking device
exclusions: Business thresholds: only a for-profit business doing business in California that had annual gross revenue above $26,625,000 in the preceding calendar year (CPI-adjusted from $25M effective 2025-01-01; next adjustment due January 2027), OR alone or in combination buys, sells, or shares personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households per year, OR derives 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information (Civ. Code 1798.140(d)(1)); entities under common branding and control, and certain joint ventures, are aggregated (1798.140(d)(2)-(3)). Exemptions (1798.145(c)(1)): medical information governed by the CMIA, and PHI collected by a HIPAA covered entity or business associate; a CMIA provider or HIPAA covered entity to the extent it maintains patient information the same way as medical information or PHI; personal information collected as part of a clinical trial or other biomedical research study subject to or conducted under the Common Rule, ICH good clinical practice guidelines, or FDA human subject protection requirements. Deidentified patient information meeting 45 CFR 164.514 and derived from patient information originally held by a HIPAA-, CMIA-, or Common Rule-regulated entity is also exempt unless reidentified (1798.146(a)(4)). Deidentified and aggregate consumer information is not personal information (1798.140). Non-profits and government agencies are not 'businesses' unless they meet the definition. A HIPAA/CMIA exemption is data- or entity-specific: a non-HIPAA consumer health app is covered by the CCPA (and may separately be a CMIA 'provider' under Civ. Code 56.06).
key_definitions: 'business' = for-profit entity doing business in California that collects consumers' personal information, determines the purposes and means of processing, and meets one of the three thresholds above (1798.140(d)(1)), plus controlled or commonly branded affiliates, qualifying joint ventures, and any person that voluntarily certifies to the CPPA (1798.140(d)(2)-(4)); 'consumer' = a natural person who is a California resident (1798.140(i)); 'personal information' includes identifiers, commercial information, biometric data, and 'personal information collected and analyzed concerning a consumer's health', and may be held in physical, digital, or abstract digital formats including AI systems capable of outputting it; excludes deidentified and aggregate consumer information (1798.140(v)); 'sensitive personal information' includes Social Security, driver's license, state ID, and passport numbers; account credentials; precise geolocation; racial or ethnic origin, citizenship or immigration status, religious or philosophical beliefs, union membership; contents of mail, email, and texts; genetic data; neural data; biometric processing to identify a consumer; health information; sex life or sexual orientation (1798.140(ae)); CPPA regulations add personal information of consumers the business knows are under 16 (11 CCR 7001(bbb)(4)); 'sell' = disclosing personal information to a third party for monetary or other valuable consideration (1798.140(ad)); 'share' = disclosing to a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising (1798.140(ah)); 'service provider' = processes personal information on behalf of a business under a written contract that bars selling/sharing and use outside the business purposes (1798.140(ag)); the CCPA has no separate defined term 'consumer health data' (health information is within personal and sensitive personal information)
key_questions: Do you meet a CCPA business route: revenue over $26,625,000, buying/selling/sharing personal information of 100,000+ California consumers or households, or half of revenue from selling or sharing it? Are you controlled by, or in a joint venture with, a business that does (1798.140(d)(2)-(4))?; Is the company a for-profit that meets a threshold (revenue above $26.6M, 100,000+ consumers or households, or 50%+ of revenue from selling/sharing)?; Are you a HIPAA covered entity or business associate, and is the data PHI?; Is the data CMIA medical information (provider, plan, contractor, or a business deemed a provider under Civ. Code 56.06)?; Is it a consumer wellness or health app outside HIPAA and CMIA?; Do you sell or share data with advertisers or third parties?; Do you collect neural, genetic, biometric, or precise-geolocation data?; Is any user known to be under 16?; Do you use ADMT for decisions about healthcare services, or process sensitive data (risk assessment duties)?
obligations: Give notice at collection; honor rights to know/access, delete, correct, opt out of sale/sharing, and limit use of sensitive personal information; follow data minimization; maintain reasonable security; do risk assessments, cybersecurity audits, and ADMT duties per CPPA regulations. Medical information governed by CMIA, PHI held by HIPAA covered entities/business associates, and CMIA providers/HIPAA covered entities that treat patient information the same way are exempt (1798.145(c)).
enforcement: CPPA administrative fines up to $2,663 per violation or $7,988 per intentional violation or violation involving a consumer known to be under 16 (1798.155; CPI-adjusted from $2,500/$7,500 effective 2025-01-01); AG civil penalties at the same adjusted amounts (1798.199.90); consumer private action for data breaches of nonencrypted personal information caused by failure to maintain reasonable security, $107-$799 per consumer per incident or actual damages, whichever is greater (1798.150; adjusted from $100-$750). Amounts are adjusted every odd-numbered January, so check for a 2027 adjustment.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: FindLaw code pages (1798.145, 1798.150, 1798.155, 1798.185, 1798.198; current as of 2026-01-01); consumer rights sections also confirmed through SB 923 chaptered text (1798.105, 1798.130). The 2023-03-29 date in the researcher notes was memory and is removed.

title: California Invasion of Privacy Act: recording of confidential communications and private right of action
effective_date_notes: Added by Stats. 1967, ch. 1509 (Invasion of Privacy Act, Pen. Code 630 et seq.); 632 amended 1976, 1985, 1990, 1992, 1994, and 2016 (ch. 855). Only the enactment year (1967) is confirmed in a source; 1967-11-08 is inferred from the 1967 regular session's common effective date (61 days after the 1967-09-08 adjournment; confirmed for another 1967 chapter), not read for ch. 1509 itself. The all-party consent duty has applied for decades either way.
triggers: A person or organization (including a health system, clinic, plan, or vendor) uses an electronic recording device or software, such as an ambient scribe, call recorder, or voice agent, to record or eavesdrop on a confidential conversation (in person, telephone, or video) without the consent of all parties.
example_tools: ambient AI scribe that records clinic or telehealth visits; AI call recorder or visit recorder for patient encounters; voice agent that handles patient phone calls and records them; call-center speech analytics on patient or member calls; AI note-taker joining telehealth video visits
exclusions: Applies only to 'confidential communications': communications carried on in circumstances that reasonably indicate a party wants them confined to the parties; excludes communications in a public gathering, in an open legislative, judicial, executive, or administrative proceeding, or in any other circumstance in which the parties may reasonably expect the communication to be overheard or recorded (Pen. Code 632(c)). No violation if all parties consent. Section 632(b) 'person' excludes a person known by all parties to be overhearing or recording. Exempts public utility companies and employees performing maintenance or operation, and telephonic systems used within correctional facilities (632(e)). No HIPAA or health-care exemption appears in the text. Section 632 requires an electronic amplifying or recording device and intent. The separate cellular/cordless phone provision is Pen. Code 632.7 (not reviewed in detail here).
key_definitions: 'person' = an individual, business association, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, or other legal entity, and an individual acting or purporting to act for or on behalf of a government (Pen. Code 632(b)); 'confidential communication' = any communication carried on in circumstances as may reasonably indicate that any party to the communication desires it to be confined to the parties thereto, excluding public gatherings, open proceedings, and circumstances where the parties may reasonably expect it to be overheard or recorded (632(c)); violation = a person who, intentionally and without the consent of all parties to a confidential communication, uses an electronic amplifying or recording device to eavesdrop upon or record the confidential communication (632(a)); evidence obtained in violation is inadmissible in judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceedings, except in prosecutions for violating the section (632(d)); private right of action: any person injured by a violation of the chapter may sue for the greater of $5,000 per violation or three times actual damages, plus injunctive relief, and need not show actual damages (637.2(a)-(c))
key_questions: Does the tool record or transcribe audio of a live conversation (in person, phone, or video) rather than only typed notes?; Is the conversation reasonably expected to be confidential (clinical visit, patient call) rather than open or expected to be recorded?; Has every party (patient, clinician, any family member or interpreter present, and the caller on a phone line) consented to the recording, and is consent obtained before recording starts?; Does the voice agent or call-recording system announce the recording at the start of every call?; Are any participants located in California, including out-of-state callers or clinicians?; Does a vendor store or use the recording for its own purposes such as model training?
obligations: Do not intentionally record, or eavesdrop on, a confidential communication using an electronic device without the consent of all parties; this applies whether the parties are in each other's presence or communicate by telephone or other device. Evidence obtained in violation is inadmissible. For AI scribes, call recorders, and voice agents, obtain consent from every participant before recording.
enforcement: Criminal under Pen. Code 632(a): fine up to $2,500 per violation and/or up to one year in county jail (state prison also possible), and up to $10,000 per violation for a person with a prior conviction under related sections. Civil under Pen. Code 637.2: any person injured by a violation may sue for the greater of $5,000 per violation or three times actual damages, plus injunctive relief; actual damages need not be shown.
notes: Tier 2 mirrors: FindLaw (632 and 637.2, current as of 2026-01-01) and california.public.law (632 subdivisions (a)-(e)); enactment (Stats. 1967 ch. 1509) and amendment years from legintent.com statutory history (Tier 3) and california.public.law. leginfo is blocked. Federal 18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d) requires only one-party consent (Cornell LII text), so California's all-party rule governs where a participant is in California. Section 632.7 separately covers recording of cellular or cordless phone communications without all-party consent. Enactment day not confirmed, hence partially_verified.

title: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act
effective_date_notes: CMIA repealed and re-added by Stats. 1981, ch. 782; operation suspended until 1982-01-01 per the Clerk of the Assembly 1981 statutes summary cited in notes (that summary was read in an earlier pass; not re-opened on 2026-10-10 because the PDF exceeds the 25 MB tool limit). Amended by AB 2089 (Ch. 690, Stats. 2022; mental health digital services), AB 254 (Ch. 254, Stats. 2023; reproductive or sexual health digital services), and AB 1979 (Ch. 854, Stats. 2026; health care chatbots, from 2027-01-01).
trigger_rule: ca_users AND (phi OR mental_health_use OR cmia_digital_service OR (consumer_health_data AND genai AND chatbot))
triggers: A licensed provider, Knox-Keene plan, pharmaceutical company, or contractor (medical group, IPA, PBM, medical service organization) creates, maintains, or discloses individually identifiable medical information of California patients; or a business offers consumers software, hardware, or an app designed to maintain medical information for individual management or for diagnosis, treatment, or management of a condition, or offers a mental health or reproductive/sexual health digital service, or (from 2027-01-01) a health care chatbot; such businesses are deemed providers for CMIA purposes.
example_tools: ambient AI scribe used by a clinic or health system; EHR or patient portal software; mental health or therapy app; reproductive or period-tracking app; consumer health chatbot or symptom checker (from 2027-01-01); personal health record or medical-records app
exclusions: Who is not covered: 'provider of health care' does not include insurance institutions as defined in Ins. Code 791.02(k) (those are governed by the Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act), and 'contractor' does not include insurance institutions or pharmaceutical benefits managers licensed under Knox-Keene (Civ. Code 56.05(e), (s)). 'Contractor' is limited to medical groups, independent practice associations, pharmaceutical benefits managers, and medical service organizations that are not plans or providers. Medical information is limited to individually identifiable information in the possession of or derived from a provider, plan, pharmaceutical company, or contractor; health data held by a business that is not one of these and not deemed a provider under 56.06 is outside the CMIA (CCPA may apply instead). A business deemed a provider under 56.06 is a provider only for the CMIA, not for other laws. Permitted disclosures without authorization include the mandatory list in 56.10(b) (court orders, subpoenas, search warrants, patient requests, coroners) and 24 permissive categories in 56.10(c) (treatment/diagnosis, payment, billing, peer review, licensing, research, public health reporting, abuse reporting, and others). Section 56.30 exempts categories of information from the Act's limits (for example certain mental health and public social services records, workers' compensation, law enforcement, and records of insurance regulators and DMHC). Health care chatbot rule applies only to a generative AI chatbot meeting all three prongs of 56.05(i).
key_definitions: 'provider of health care' = a person licensed or certified under B&P Division 2 (500 et seq.), the Osteopathic or Chiropractic Initiative Acts, or H&S Division 2.5 (EMS), or a clinic, health dispensary, or health facility licensed under H&S Division 2 (1200 et seq.); excludes insurance institutions (Civ. Code 56.05(s)); 'contractor' = a medical group, independent practice association, pharmaceutical benefits manager, or medical service organization that is not a health care service plan or provider of health care; excludes insurance institutions and Knox-Keene-licensed PBMs (56.05(e)); 'medical information' = individually identifiable information, in electronic or physical form, in possession of or derived from a provider of health care, health care service plan, pharmaceutical company, or contractor regarding a patient's medical history, mental health application information, reproductive or sexual health application information, mental or physical condition, or treatment; 'individually identifiable' = includes any element sufficient to identify the person, such as name, address, email, phone, or SSN, or information that alone or combined with public information reveals identity; immigration status and place of birth collected with such information is treated as medical information (56.05(m)); 'mental health digital service' = a mobile app or website that collects mental health application information from a consumer, markets itself as facilitating mental health services, and uses the information to facilitate those services (56.05(o)); 'mental health application information' = information related to a consumer's inferred or diagnosed mental health or substance use disorder collected by a mental health digital service (56.05(n)); 'reproductive or sexual health digital service' (56.05(u)); 'health care chatbot' = generative AI system with a natural language interface that provides adaptive, human-like responses, is marketed as facilitating or supporting health services, and uses health information the consumer provides, allows access to, or that the chatbot collects, generates, or infers (56.05(i), from 2027-01-01 per AB 1979); deemed providers (Civ. Code 56.06): (a) a business organized to maintain medical information so individuals or providers can access it or to manage it or for diagnosis and treatment; (b) a business offering software or hardware (including mobile apps) to consumers designed to maintain medical information for individual management or for diagnosis, treatment, or management of a medical condition; (c) licensed cannabis businesses receiving medical cannabis identification cards or physician recommendations; (d) a business offering a mental health digital service; (e) a reproductive or sexual health digital service; (f) a business offering a health care chatbot; businesses deemed providers must maintain the same confidentiality standards and are subject to the Act's penalties (56.06(g), (h)); 'authorization' = permission under 56.11 or 56.21 (56.05(b)); 'patient' = a natural person, living or not, who received health care services from a provider and to whom medical information pertains (56.05(p)). Subdivision letters for 56.05 follow the AB 1979 text operative 2027-01-01, which inserts new definitions (a), (h), (i); before 2027-01-01 the same definitions carry earlier letters.
key_questions: Is the organization a licensed provider, a Knox-Keene plan, a pharmaceutical company, or a contractor (medical group, IPA, PBM, medical service organization)?; If it is a software or app company, is the product designed to maintain medical information so users or providers can access or manage it, or for diagnosis, treatment, or management of a condition (56.06(b))?; Is it a mental health or reproductive/sexual health app or website (56.06(d), (e))?; Is it a generative AI chatbot marketed to support health services that uses users' health information (56.06(f), from 2027-01-01)?; Is the data individually identifiable and tied to a medical history, condition, or treatment?; Does a patient authorization or a 56.10(b)/(c) exception cover each disclosure, sale, or marketing use?; Are you an insurance institution (outside the CMIA, covered by the Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act)?; If you build an EHR/EMR, does the system preserve integrity and an audit trail of changes (56.101(b))?
obligations: Providers, plans, and contractors may not disclose medical information without patient authorization unless an exception applies (Civ. Code 56.10); businesses offering software or hardware to maintain medical information, mental health or reproductive health digital services, and (from 2027) health care chatbots are deemed providers and must meet the same confidentiality standards (56.06).
enforcement: Private action for nominal damages of $1,000 and actual damages for negligent release; administrative fines and civil penalties from $2,500 up to $250,000 per violation depending on intent and financial gain (Civ. Code 56.36).
notes: Whole instrument included (criterion C). Obligations and penalties confirmed via Tier 2 mirror FindLaw (56.10, 56.36, current as of 2026-01-01) and the AB 1979 chaptered text (56.05, 56.06). Amendment bills confirmed via Digital Democracy. Operative date: Stats. 1981 ch. 782, operation suspended until 1982-01-01 (Clerk of the Assembly, 1981 statutes summary: https://clerk.assembly.ca.gov/sites/clerk.assembly.ca.gov/files/archive/Statutes/1981/81Vol4_Summary.pdf).

title: CPPA regulations: automated decisionmaking technology, risk assessments, cybersecurity audits
citation: 11 CCR 7001 et seq.; Art. 9 cybersecurity audits (7120-7124), Art. 10 risk assessments (7150-7157), Art. 11 ADMT (7200-7222)
effective_date_notes: Regulations effective 2026-01-01. ADMT: businesses using ADMT for significant decisions before 2027-01-01 must comply by 2027-01-01 (7200(b)). Risk assessments for existing processing due by 2027-12-31, first submissions by 2028-04-01 (7155, 7157). First cybersecurity audit reports due 2028-04-01 / 2029-04-01 / 2030-04-01 by revenue tier (7121).
trigger_rule: ca_users AND ccpa_business AND non_hipaa_personal_info AND (automated_significant_decision OR shares_personal_data OR consumer_health_data OR neural_data)
triggers: A CCPA business (outside the HIPAA PHI and CMIA exemptions) uses technology that processes personal information and replaces or substantially replaces human decisionmaking (no qualifying human involvement) to make a 'significant decision' about a California consumer, including the provision or denial of healthcare services (diagnosis, prevention, treatment, or assessment or care of an individual's health); separately, a business must do a risk assessment before selling or sharing personal information, processing sensitive personal information (including health data), using ADMT for a significant decision, or training ADMT or facial/emotion-recognition tools on consumers' data, and must complete cybersecurity audits if it meets the 7120(b) thresholds.
example_tools: AI prior-authorization or coverage-eligibility decision engine used by a CCPA-covered business; algorithm that decides whether a consumer is offered or denied a health service or program; automated triage or eligibility screening for a non-HIPAA digital health service; AI that assigns patients to care tiers without clinician review; consumer health app that uses sensitive health data to make automated determinations
exclusions: Reaches only CCPA 'businesses' (for-profit; revenue above $26,625,000, or 100,000+ consumers or households, or 50%+ of revenue from selling/sharing; Civ. Code 1798.140(d)); medical information governed by the CMIA and PHI held by HIPAA covered entities and business associates stay outside the CCPA (1798.145(c)), so most clinical tools run by HIPAA entities are outside these rules. Technology is not 'ADMT' unless it replaces or substantially replaces human decisionmaking; a decision with qualifying 'human involvement' (reviewer who knows how to interpret the output, reviews and analyzes the output and other relevant information, and has authority to make or change the decision) is not ADMT use (7001(e)(1)). ADMT excludes web hosting, domain registration, networking, caching, website loading, data storage, firewalls, anti-virus, anti-malware, spam and robocall filtering, spellchecking, calculators, databases, and spreadsheets, provided they do not replace human decisionmaking (7001(e)(3)). 'Significant decision' excludes advertising to a consumer (7001(ddd)(6)). Opt-out of ADMT is not required where the business offers a human appeal to a designated reviewer with authority to overturn the decision (7221(b)(1)), or for admission/hiring and work allocation/compensation uses meeting the conditions in 7221(b)(2)-(3) (not healthcare). Risk-assessment carve-out: employee sensitive data processed solely for compensation, work authorization, benefits, accommodation, or wage reporting (7150(b)(2)(A)). Cybersecurity audits apply only above the thresholds in 7120(b).
key_definitions: 'automated decisionmaking technology' (ADMT) = any technology that processes personal information and uses computation to replace human decisionmaking or substantially replace human decisionmaking; 'substantially replace' = a business uses the technology's output to make a decision without human involvement; includes profiling that replaces or substantially replaces human decisionmaking (11 CCR 7001(e)); 'human involvement' = the human reviewer must (A) know how to interpret and use the output, (B) review and analyze the output and any other relevant information, and (C) have authority to make or change the decision (7001(e)(1)); 'significant decision' = a decision that results in the provision or denial of financial or lending services, housing, education enrollment or opportunities, employment or independent contracting opportunities or compensation, or healthcare services (7001(ddd)); 'healthcare services' = services related to the diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of human disease or impairment, or the assessment or care of an individual's health (7001(ddd)(5)); 'sensitive personal information' includes personal information collected and analyzed concerning a consumer's health, sex life, or sexual orientation, neural and genetic data, and personal information of consumers known to be under 16 (7001(bbb)); risk assessment is required before: selling or sharing personal information; processing sensitive personal information; using ADMT for a significant decision; certain automated inference of health, behavior, or performance from systematic observation in education or employment contexts or at sensitive locations; or processing personal information to train ADMT for a significant decision or facial-recognition, emotion-recognition, or similar technology (7150(b)); 'train' (7001(fff)); compliance date for ADMT used before 2027-01-01 is 2027-01-01 (7200(b))
key_questions: Is the company a CCPA business, and is the data outside the HIPAA PHI and CMIA exemptions?; Does the tool use personal information to make or drive a decision about whether a consumer gets or is denied healthcare services (or credit, housing, education, or employment)?; Does a human reviewer with authority, who understands the output and reviews other information, make or change the decision (then it is not ADMT)?; Do you offer a human appeal that can overturn the decision (opt-out exception)?; Do you process sensitive personal information, sell or share data, or train models on consumers' data (risk assessment trigger)?; Do you meet the revenue and consumer-count thresholds for a cybersecurity audit?; Did you start using ADMT before 2027-01-01?
obligations: For ADMT used in significant decisions: give a pre-use notice, offer an opt-out (with exceptions), and answer access requests with plain-language explanations of purpose and logic. Conduct risk assessments before significant-risk processing, retain them, and submit information to the CPPA. Complete annual independent cybersecurity audits where thresholds are met.
enforcement: CPPA and AG enforcement under CCPA.
notes: Tier 1: cppa.ca.gov rulemaking page (OAL approval and SOS filing 2025-09-22; effective 2026-01-01) and approved regulation text PDF (cppa.ca.gov/regulations/pdf/ccpa_updates_cyber_risk_admt_appr_text.pdf). OAL approval date corrected from 2025-09-23. CCPA exemptions for CMIA/HIPAA data still apply.

title: Civil Rights Council employment automated-decision system regulations (FEHA)
citation: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 2, 11008 (definitions, including 'agent'), 11008.1 (automated-decision systems), 11009(f) (unlawful use of ADS or selection criteria; anti-bias testing evidence), 11013 (recordkeeping, four years), 11016-11017 (pre-employment practices and employee selection, as they reach ADS); section numbers taken from the Civil Rights Council 2025-03-17 text of the proposed regulations, not the final adopted text
triggers: An employer regularly employing five or more individuals, or its agent (such as a staffing, recruiting, or screening vendor), uses an automated-decision system (including AI, algorithms, or data-driven assessments) to make or facilitate decisions about hiring, promotion, pay, benefits, or other employment benefits for applicants or employees in California, including at health-care employers.
example_tools: AI resume screener or candidate ranking tool used by a health system; video interview analysis software (facial expression, word choice, voice) used to hire clinicians or staff; online skills or personality assessment or game used in hiring nurses or technicians; AI workforce scheduling or performance scoring tool that affects employment benefits; applicant-recruiting ad targeting tool
exclusions: Employment context only: not a patient-facing or clinical-care rule. Covers employers regularly employing five or more individuals and their agents (2 CCR 11008, definition of 'employer'). The ADS definition excludes word processing and spreadsheet software, map navigation, web hosting, domain registration, networking, caching, website loading, data storage, firewalls, anti-virus, anti-malware, spam and robocall filtering, spellchecking, calculators, and databases or similar technologies, provided they do not make a decision regarding an employment benefit (11008.1(a)(2)). Section numbers here come from the Council's 2025-03-17 pre-adoption text; the final adopted text is a scanned image and was not machine-checked.
key_definitions: 'automated-decision system' = a computational process that makes a decision or facilitates human decisionmaking regarding an employment benefit; may be derived from or use AI, machine learning, algorithms, statistics, or other data processing; tasks include computer-based assessments or tests (questions, puzzles, games) to make predictive assessments or screen and evaluate applicants or employees, directing job ads to targeted groups, screening resumes for terms or patterns, analyzing facial expression, word choice, or voice in online interviews, and analyzing applicant or employee data acquired from third parties (2 CCR 11008.1(a)); 'agent' = any person acting on behalf of an employer, directly or indirectly, to exercise a function traditionally exercised by the employer or any other FEHA-regulated activity (such as recruitment, screening, hiring, promotion, pay, benefits, or leave decisions), including through an ADS; an agent of an employer is also an 'employer' under the Act (11008(b)); 'automated-decision system data' = data used in or resulting from an ADS, and data used to develop or customize an ADS for a particular employer (11008.1(d)); anti-bias testing evidence (or lack of it) is relevant to a discrimination claim or defense (11009(f)); employment records including ADS data must be kept four years (11013)
key_questions: Is the tool used to recruit, screen, assess, rank, hire, promote, or make pay, benefit, or leave decisions about applicants or employees (not patients)?; Does the employer regularly employ five or more people?; Is a vendor acting as the employer's agent in running the tool?; Does an assessment, game, or question set elicit information about a disability or other protected trait?; Have you done and documented anti-bias testing?; Do you keep ADS data and employment records for four years?
obligations: Using an automated-decision system that harms applicants or employees based on protected characteristics may violate FEHA; ADS assessments that elicit disability information may be unlawful medical inquiries; keep employment records, including automated-decision data, for at least four years.
enforcement: Civil Rights Department under FEHA.
notes: Employment ADS rule included per inclusion edge cases; tag narrowly. Approval 2025-06-27 and effective 2025-10-01 confirmed on the official CRD release (Tier 1). Final text and OAL notice PDFs are scanned images with no text layer, so CCR section numbers and full obligations were not checked against the text.
