title: California AI Transparency Act amendments (2026)
effective_date_notes: Urgency statute (SEC. 8), effective on approval 2026-09-30. Assistive-technology exemption until 2029-01-01; $50,000 penalty for false assistive-technology claims sunsets 2029-01-01.
trigger_rule: ca_users AND generates_media AND (trains_genai_model OR NOT third_party_model)
triggers: A person creates, codes, or produces a publicly accessible generative AI system in California that can create or alter image, video, or audio content (1,000,000 monthly user threshold removed), or licenses such a system to others.
example_tools: AI tool that generates or edits patient-education videos or images; AI voice cloning or synthetic speech for a health app; generative medical illustration tool; AI avatar telehealth explainer videos; synthetic medical image generator
exclusions: Does not apply to products, services, websites, or apps providing exclusively non-user-generated video games (B&P 22757.5(a)); before 2029-01-01, does not apply to GenAI systems designed to primarily function as assistive technology (22757.5(b)); latent disclosures cover image, video, and audio content created or altered by the system, except by minor modification, and only to the extent technically feasible (22757.3(a)); the verification tool may be a compliant third-party tool (22757.2(e)); covered providers need not monitor licensees (22757.3(b)(5)).
key_definitions: 'covered provider' = a person that creates, codes, or otherwise produces a generative AI system that is publicly accessible within California (B&P 22757.1(e)); 'GenAI system' = AI that can generate derived synthetic content, including text, images, video, and audio (22757.1(g)); 'provenance data' = information about the origin and modification history of digital content in a format compliant or interoperable with widely adopted standards (22757.1(n)); 'system provenance data' = provenance data not reasonably capable of being associated with a particular user, describing the device, system, or service used or content authenticity (22757.1(o)); 'minor modification' = brightness, contrast, color, sharpening, saturating, resizing, scaling, cropping, format conversion, audio denoising (22757.1(l)); 'assistive technology' (22757.1(b))
key_questions: Does your publicly accessible generative AI create or alter images, video, or audio?; Did you build or produce the system, or do you license it from someone else?; Do you license your system to others?; Do you claim it is assistive technology, and is it designed primarily for that?; Does your verification tool or service collect personal information beyond what is strictly necessary?
obligations: Covered providers (any publicly accessible GenAI system; user threshold removed) must embed latent disclosures (provider, system/version, time, unique ID, whether created or altered) in image, video, and audio content except minor modifications; offer a free disclosure verification tool (or direct users to a compliant third-party tool) without over-collecting personal information; if a covered provider knows that an identifiable third-party licensee modified a licensed GenAI system so it no longer complies, the provider must, within 72 hours of discovering it, either terminate the license or notify the licensee of its noncompliance and of the reporting requirement (22757.3(b)(2)); a notified licensee must bring the system into compliance or stop using or offering it, and report which it did to the provider within 96 hours of receiving the notice ((b)(3)); if the provider gets no report, or the report says the licensee did neither, the provider must report the licensee's noncompliance to the Attorney General (no deadline stated) ((b)(4)); providers need not monitor or investigate licensees ((b)(5)); not falsely claim assistive-technology status.
enforcement: $5,000 per violation per day (AG, city attorneys, county counsel); $50,000 per violation for false assistive-technology claims until 2029-01-01. Pending actions over conduct that is no longer a violation cannot be maintained.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 861, Stats. 2026; approved by Governor 2026-09-30; urgency clause adopted in both houses and stated in SEC. 8. The manifest-disclosure option was removed. AB 2713 (Ch. 856) is a companion amending platform duties; no separate row.

title: Adam's Law (companion chatbot child safety)
effective_date_notes: Age-assurance duty (21811) effective 2027-01-01; risk assessment, child safety policy, crisis protocol, defaults, and ad/data limits (21812, 21813) operative 2027-07-01; interface testing by 2028-01-01; first independent child safety audit by 2029-01-01 (AB 1405-contingent version operative because AB 1405 was chaptered as Ch. 178, Stats. 2026); operators under $500M revenue exempt from audits before 2032-01-01.
triggers: An operator offers a companion chatbot in California that children can access.
example_tools: AI companion or 'AI friend' app teens can download; emotional-support or anxiety chatbot for adolescents; character chatbot platform open to under-18 users; AI study buddy with a persistent persona and memory; mental health companion bot for teens
exclusions: 'Operator' excludes a postsecondary educational institution offering a companion chatbot exclusively for educational settings, and an entity offering one exclusively to employees, contractors, or other personnel for workplace use (21810.5(j)(2)); except for age assurance (21811), the age-assurance description for operators that bar children (21812(b)), and enforcement (21816), the chapter applies only to operators who allow child users after age determination (21810.5(j)(1)(B)); bots outside the SB 243 'companion chatbot' definition (customer service, productivity, internal research, technical assistance, limited video-game bots, stand-alone voice assistants) are not covered (21810.5(f), 22601(b)); the bar on diagnosing or treating a child's health does not apply to a chatbot designed for those purposes and regulated by FDA as a medical device and under HIPAA (21812(d)(5)(A)(ii)); product recommendations the user explicitly requests are not barred advertising (21812(d)(5)(A)(ix)(II)); operators with under $500M prior-year gross revenue are exempt from child safety audits before 2032-01-01 (21814); age-appropriate information about abuse, neglect, or bullying is not barred (21812(d)(5)(B)).
key_definitions: 'child' = a natural person under 18 (B&P 21810.5(a)); 'companion chatbot' = as defined in 22601 (21810.5(f)); 'operator' = a person who makes a companion chatbot available to a user in the state, with the postsecondary-education and workplace-only exclusions (21810.5(j)); 'covered harm' = reasonably foreseeable physical or financial harm, severe and reasonably foreseeable psychological or emotional harm to a reasonable child, highly offensive privacy intrusion, or unlawful adverse discrimination caused by a child's use (21810.5(g)); 'child safety risk' = reasonably foreseeable risk of a covered harm to a child (21810.5(d)); 'persistent conversational memory' = use of prior conversations in future ones, excluding information needed for child safety, user identification, preferences, or device configuration (21810.5(m)); 'substantial modification' = new version, release, or update that materially changes functionality or performance (21810.5(o)); 'parent' = parent or legal guardian, not for an emancipated youth (21810.5(k))
key_questions: Does the product meet the SB 243 'companion chatbot' definition (human-like, meets social needs, sustains a relationship)?; Is it available to users in California?; Do you allow users under 18 once age is determined, or do you block them?; How do you determine user age?; Is it offered only in a university educational setting or only to your own workforce?; Does the bot discuss health, diagnose, or suggest treatment, and is it an FDA-regulated medical device?; Does it use persistent memory, push notifications, ads, or sell or share user data?; Was prior-year gross revenue under $500M (audit timing)?
obligations: Determine user age (or apply child protections to all users); before releasing a new or substantially modified companion chatbot, perform and document a child-safety risk assessment and mitigate risks; publish a child safety policy; for child users, run a crisis-response protocol (988 access or parent notification), parent-only default settings (no persistent memory or push notifications, 1-hour session and 2-hour daily limits), periodic AI disclosure, and reasonable measures to stop the bot from encouraging self-harm or disordered eating, attempting to diagnose or treat the child's health (unless the chatbot is designed for that purpose and regulated by FDA as a medical device and under HIPAA), claiming sentience, or simulating romance; no behavioral ads to or sale of children's data; independent child safety audits.
enforcement: Public prosecutors: civil penalties up to $5,000 per affected child (negligent) and $15,000 per affected child (intentional); AG injunctive relief; private action by a child (or parent) for actual harm from violations of 21812(d)(1)-(5); no UCL private action.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 190, Stats. 2026; approved by Governor 2026-09-10 (gov.ca.gov 9/10/2026 release). Default effective 2027-01-01 with later operative dates as noted. The annual-risk-assessment wording was not found; assessments are tied to new or substantially modified releases.

title: Physicians Make Decisions Act (utilization review AI limits)
trigger_rule: ca_users AND utilization_review AND (org_plan OR org_developer)
triggers: A health care service plan or disability insurer (or its contractor) uses AI, algorithms, or other software to help decide utilization review or management, including approve, modify, delay, or deny of services based on medical necessity.
example_tools: AI prior-authorization reviewer for a health plan; algorithm that auto-scores medical-necessity requests; utilization management vendor's AI concurrent-review tool; claims or UM software that recommends approve or deny; AI tool that flags requests for retrospective review
exclusions: Applies only to Knox-Keene health care service plans (including specialized plans) and disability insurers covering hospital, medical, or surgical expenses, and entities they contract or delegate UR/UM to (H&S 1367.01(a), (k); Ins. Code 10123.135(a), (j)); applies only to utilization review or management based in whole or in part on medical necessity of covered health care services (1367.01(k)(1), (4)); does not apply to providers' own use of AI for clinical care; the tool may still assist, but cannot itself deny, delay, or modify care on medical-necessity grounds (1367.01(k)(2)).
key_definitions: 'artificial intelligence' = an engineered or machine-based system that varies in autonomy and infers from input how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments (H&S 1367.01(k)(3); Ins. Code 10123.135(j)(3)); covered use = 'an artificial intelligence, algorithm, or other software tool for the purpose of utilization review or utilization management functions, based in whole or in part on medical necessity' that prospectively, retrospectively, or concurrently reviews requests for covered services (1367.01(k)(1), (4)); determination of medical necessity may be made only by a 'licensed physician or a licensed health care professional competent to evaluate the specific clinical issues' (1367.01(k)(2))
key_questions: Is the user a Knox-Keene health plan, a disability insurer covering hospital/medical/surgical costs, or a vendor or medical group performing delegated UR/UM for one?; Does the tool review prior, concurrent, or retrospective requests for covered services based on medical necessity?; Can the tool deny, delay, or modify a request without a licensed clinician's determination?; Does it use the individual enrollee's clinical history and circumstances or only group data?; Is the tool disclosed in written UR policies and open to DMHC/DHCS or CDI audit?
obligations: When a plan or disability insurer (or a contracted UR/UM entity) uses AI, algorithms, or software for utilization review based on medical necessity, the tool must base determinations on the enrollee's own clinical history and circumstances (not solely group datasets), not supplant provider decision-making, not discriminate, be fairly applied, be open to audit by the regulator, be disclosed in written UR policies, be periodically reviewed, not use patient data beyond its stated purpose, and not directly or indirectly cause harm to the enrollee. The tool may not deny, delay, or modify care based on medical necessity; only a licensed physician or competent licensed health professional may make that determination.
enforcement: DMHC (administrative penalties under H&S Code 1367.01) for health care service plans; Department of Insurance for disability insurers; DHCS audit access for Medi-Cal plans.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 879, Stats. 2024; approved by Governor 2024-09-28 (DD history matches gov.ca.gov 9.28.24 update; the 2024-09-30 date in one secondary source is wrong). Default effective 2025-01-01.

title: Consumer privacy: sensitive personal information: neural data
citation: Civil Code 1798.140(ae) (sensitive personal information: neural data)
triggers: A business covered by the CCPA collects or processes neural data (brain/nervous system activity), e.g. through wellness or neurotech devices.
example_tools: EEG or brain-sensing wellness headband; neurofeedback or meditation device that records brain activity; consumer neurotechnology app used for sleep, focus, or mood; EMG or nerve-signal wearable; brain-computer interface research product sold to consumers
exclusions: Only changes the CCPA definition of sensitive personal information, so it reaches only CCPA 'businesses' (revenue above $26,625,000, 100,000+ consumers or households, or 50%+ of revenue from selling/sharing; Civ. Code 1798.140(d)). Medical information governed by the CMIA, PHI held by HIPAA covered entities and business associates, and certain clinical research data remain exempt from the CCPA (1798.145(c), 1798.146). Neural data is information 'generated by measuring the activity of a consumer's central or peripheral nervous system' and 'not inferred from nonneural information', so inferences about mental states drawn from non-neural inputs (typing, heart rate, voice) are not neural data. Sensitive personal information excludes publicly available information.
key_definitions: 'neural data' = information that is generated by measuring the activity of a consumer's central or peripheral nervous system, and that is not inferred from nonneural information (Civ. Code 1798.140(ae)(1)(G)); 'sensitive personal information' = personal information that reveals listed categories (including neural data, genetic data, precise geolocation, health information, and others) (1798.140(ae)); 'business' = see CA-CCPA thresholds (1798.140(d)); SB 1223 SEC. 1.5 is the operative version of 1798.140 because it was chaptered after AB 1008
key_questions: Does the device or app measure activity of the central or peripheral nervous system (EEG, EMG, nerve signals)?; Is the company a CCPA business over the thresholds?; Is the data held by a HIPAA covered entity or business associate, or is it CMIA medical information (exempt), or a consumer neurotech product (covered)?; Do you infer mental states only from non-neural data?; Do you give notice of the collection and honor limit-use requests for sensitive personal information?
obligations: Neural data (information generated by measuring central or peripheral nervous system activity, not inferred from nonneural information) is sensitive personal information under the CCPA, so CCPA notice and right-to-limit duties for sensitive personal information apply.
enforcement: CPPA and AG under CCPA.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 887, Stats. 2024; approved by Governor 2024-09-28. SB 1223 SEC. 1.5 (double-jointing with AB 1008) is the operative version because SB 1223 was chaptered after AB 1008. General privacy amendment; ai_specific=no.

title: Companion chatbots
effective_date_notes: Annual reporting to Office of Suicide Prevention begins 2027-07-01. Minor-specific duties in 22602(c) deleted by SB 1119 (2026) effective 2027-01-01.
triggers: An operator offers a companion chatbot (human-like, sustains relationships over time) to users in California, including emotional-support or wellness bots.
example_tools: AI companion app for loneliness or anxiety; emotional-support chatbot with a persistent persona; AI friend or 'virtual girlfriend/boyfriend' app; wellness coaching bot that remembers users across sessions and builds rapport; character chatbot platform
exclusions: Not a 'companion chatbot': a bot used only for customer service, business operational purposes, productivity and analysis of source information, internal research, or technical assistance (22601(b)(2)(A)); a video-game bot limited to game-related replies that cannot discuss mental health, self-harm, or sexually explicit conduct or hold unrelated dialogue (22601(b)(2)(B)); a stand-alone smart speaker/voice assistant that does not sustain a relationship across interactions or generate outputs likely to elicit emotional responses (22601(b)(2)(C)). The text has no health-care, clinical, or symptom-triage exclusion: a health or triage bot is outside only if it fails the base definition (not capable of meeting a user's social needs, e.g. no anthropomorphic persona or relationship across interactions) or is used only for one of the listed purposes such as customer service; a bot that also does anything beyond those purposes does not get the 'only' exclusion (reading of the text). The AI-disclosure duty in 22602(a) applies only where a reasonable person would be misled into thinking the bot is human. The known-minor duties (22602(c)) are deleted from 2027-01-01 by SB 1119.
key_definitions: 'companion chatbot' = an AI system with a natural language interface that provides adaptive, human-like responses and is capable of meeting a user's social needs, including by exhibiting anthropomorphic features and sustaining a relationship across multiple interactions; excludes customer-service/operational/productivity/research/technical-assistance bots, limited video-game bots, and stand-alone voice assistants (B&P 22601(b)); 'operator' = a person who makes a companion chatbot platform available to a user in California (22601(e)); 'companion chatbot platform' = a platform that allows a user to engage with companion chatbots (22601(c)); 'artificial intelligence' = engineered or machine-based system that infers from input how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments (22601(a))
key_questions: Does the bot give adaptive, human-like responses and can it meet users' social needs (persona, anthropomorphic features)?; Does it sustain a relationship across multiple sessions (memory, continuity)?; Is it used only for customer service, business operations, productivity, internal research, or technical support?; Is it available to users in California?; Could a reasonable user think they are talking to a human?; Do you know that any user is a minor?; Does it discuss suicide, self-harm, or mental health with users?
obligations: Operators must give a clear notice that the chatbot is AI where a reasonable person could be misled; maintain and publish a protocol to prevent suicidal ideation/self-harm content, including crisis-line referrals; disclose that companion chatbots may not be suitable for some minors; and report annually to the Office of Suicide Prevention from 2027-07-01. For known minors (until 2027-01-01, see notes): disclose AI, give 3-hourly break reminders, and take reasonable measures to prevent the chatbot from producing sexually explicit visual material or directly telling the minor to engage in sexually explicit conduct.
enforcement: Private right of action for a person who suffers injury in fact from a violation (22605): injunction, damages of the greater of actual damages or $1,000 per violation, and attorney's fees and costs.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 677, Stats. 2025; approved by Governor 2025-10-13. No urgency clause, so effective 2026-01-01 (the "upon signing" claim in one secondary source is wrong). SB 1119 (2026) amends 22602 to remove the known-minor duties, replaced by Adam's Law (B&P 21810 et seq.).

title: Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act modernization
citation: Insurance Code 791 et seq. (new Article 6.6, Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act)
effective_date_notes: Statute effective 2027-01-01 (no urgency clause; default date). New Article 6.6 operative 2028-07-01 (791.41); the existing article becomes inoperative 2028-07-01. Commissioner must adopt regulations applying key sections to producers by 2029-01-01.
trigger_rule: ca_users AND ((plan_doi_insurer AND (org_plan OR org_developer)) OR (org_developer AND utilization_review AND NOT hipaa_entity))
triggers: An insurer, producer, surplus line insurer, reinsurer, or their third-party service provider processes or shares California consumers' personal information in connection with personal, family, or household insurance (e.g., underwriting, claims, marketing), including through AI models. CMIA providers and HIPAA covered entities/business associates are exempt, except DOI-licensed disability insurers transacting health insurance (not Knox-Keene plans), which are covered.
example_tools: AI underwriting model for life, disability, or long-term care insurance; insurer chatbot that collects health information from applicants; claims-triage AI for a disability insurer; insurance producer's lead-scoring tool using consumer data; vendor analytics platform processing insurer customer data
exclusions: Does not apply to CMIA-governed providers of health care or HIPAA covered entities and business associates (Ins. Code 791.01(e)(1)), and those entities are not 'third-party service providers' (791.01(e)(2)); but it does apply to DOI-licensed disability insurers transacting health insurance that are not Knox-Keene plans (791.01(e)(4)); does not apply to title insurance (791.01(f)); applies only to processing or sharing in connection with insurance for personal, family, or household purposes, not business or professional insurance (791.01(g)); excludes SEC-regulated brokers, dealers, investment companies, advisers, and GLBA depository institutions unless DOI-licensed (791.01(d)); excludes out-of-state purchasing/risk retention groups, out-of-state assuming insurers, and foreign surplus line insurers from 'licensee' (791.02); personal information excludes aggregated, deidentified, and publicly available information.
key_definitions: 'consumer' = a California resident whose personal information is processed or shared in the business of insurance, including applicants, claimants, beneficiaries, policyholders, insureds, and certificate holders; 'licensee' = a person licensed or required to be licensed under the Insurance Code, including insurers and producers; 'third-party service provider' = a person contracting with a licensee, surplus line insurer, or reinsurer that processes or has access to personal information, including insurance support organizations; 'personal information' = information processed or shared in the business of insurance that identifies or could reasonably be linked to a consumer or household, including in abstract digital formats such as AI systems capable of outputting personal information; excludes aggregated, deidentified, and publicly available information (all Ins. Code 791.02 as amended by SB 354)
key_questions: Is the plan licensed by the California Department of Insurance as a health (disability) insurer (covered), or by DMHC as a Knox-Keene plan (exempt)?; Are you a DOI-licensed insurer, producer, surplus line insurer, reinsurer, or a vendor processing their consumers' data?; Are you a HIPAA covered entity or business associate, or a CMIA provider (exempt), or a DOI-licensed disability insurer selling health insurance (covered)?; Is the insurance for personal, family, or household purposes?; Do you share consumer data for purposes unrelated to the insurance transaction (opt-in needed)?; Does your AI model make or support adverse underwriting decisions?
obligations: Data minimization; notices of information practices; prior opt-in consent for most sharing unrelated to the insurance transaction; consumer access, correction, and deletion rights; reasons for adverse underwriting decisions; retention/destruction policies and vendor contract controls. Keep evidence of compliance for the activity year plus five calendar years, and keep consumer consents and representative notices for as long as the consumer relationship continues (791.37).
enforcement: Department of Insurance.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 481, Stats. 2026; approved by Governor 2026-09-27. Includes "AI systems capable of outputting personal information" in the personal information definition. Inclusion is borderline (insurance privacy law with AI-relevant definitions). The five-year retention duty is in 791.37 (read 2026-10-12).

title: Health care services: artificial intelligence (bias in clinical decision support)
effective_date_notes: No operative-date clause in chaptered text; default 2027-01-01. Final text contains no independent-audit requirement.
trigger_rule: ca_users AND cdss AND (org_provider OR org_developer)
triggers: A developer builds, or a deployer (defined as a health facility, clinic, physician's office, or group practice) uses, an AI clinical decision support system (prediction, classification, recommendation, or analysis aiding timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment) in health programs or activities. Health plans are not "deployers" under this section.
example_tools: sepsis prediction model in the EHR; AI readmission or deterioration risk score used by care teams; AI radiology or dermatology image classifier that flags findings; clinical recommendation engine for treatment selection; AI triage-acuity scoring tool in the emergency department
exclusions: 'Deployer' covers only health facilities, clinics, solo physician offices, and group practice offices that use a CDS system, so health plans, payers, and consumer apps are not deployers (22758(c)(5)); 'clinical decision support system' excludes appointment management (booking, canceling, rescheduling), appointment reminders, patient education and previsit materials, and payment processing, to the extent no professional license is required (22758(c)(4)); a deployer that also develops a CDS system for internal use need not generate the developer documentation in (a)(3)(B) if equivalent information is readily available to it (22758(a)(7)); duties attach only to CDS systems with a known or reasonably foreseeable risk of biased impacts in health programs or activities (22758(a)(1)). Compliance is not a defense to a discrimination claim (22758(d)).
key_definitions: 'clinical decision support system' = an AI system that produces a prediction, classification, recommendation, evaluation, or analysis that aids clinical decisionmaking related to timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment; excludes appointment management, reminders, patient education/previsit materials, and payment processing where no license is needed (B&P 22758(c)(4)); 'deployer' = a health facility, clinic, physician's office, or office of a group practice that uses a CDS system (22758(c)(5)); 'developer' = a person, partnership, state or local agency, corporation, or deployer that designs, codes, substantially modifies, or otherwise produces a CDS system for commercial or public use (22758(c)(6)); 'biased impact' = an adverse impact, including diminished access to care, quality of care, or outcomes, on an individual based on protected characteristics (22758(c)(2)); 'protected characteristic' = characteristics listed in Civ. Code 51(b) (22758(c)(11)); 'artificial intelligence' per Gov. Code 11546.45.5 (22758(c)(1))
key_questions: Does the tool produce predictions, classifications, recommendations, evaluations, or analyses that aid decisions on timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment?; Is it only for scheduling, reminders, patient education, or payment processing?; Are you building it for commercial or public use (developer), or using it as a health facility, clinic, or physician/group practice (deployer), or both?; Is there a known or reasonably foreseeable risk that it has biased impacts on patients by protected characteristic?; If you are a provider organization that built it in-house, is it for internal use only?
obligations: Developers and deployers must make reasonable efforts to identify CDS systems with known or reasonably foreseeable risk of biased impacts. Developers must mitigate those risks and give deployers a statement of intended uses and risks plus documentation on training data (including demographic representativeness), evaluation, data governance, known bias risks, and recommended use and monitoring. Deployers must regularly monitor identified systems and take reasonable, proportionate mitigation steps.
enforcement: No enforcement mechanism in the section; compliance is not a defense to a discrimination claim.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 857, Stats. 2026; approved by Governor 2026-09-30 (also gov.ca.gov 9.30.2026 AI release). Removed utilization_management tag and "health plan" from triggers: the deployer definition covers only facilities, clinics, and physician offices. The earlier-version 2030 audit schedule is not in the chaptered text.

title: Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act
citation: Business & Professions Code 22757.10-22757.16; Government Code 11546.8; Labor Code 1107 et seq.
effective_date_notes: No urgency clause; effective 2026-01-01. CalCompute (Gov. Code 11546.8) operative only upon appropriation.
triggers: A developer trains a frontier model (more than 10^26 operations); "large frontier developers" (more than $500M annual revenue with affiliates) carry extra duties.
example_tools: frontier foundation model trained with more than 10^26 operations; general-purpose LLM from a major lab that health apps build on; large multimodal model offered via API to health companies
exclusions: Does not reach developers who have not trained (or initiated training of) a frontier model above 10^26 operations, so health AI companies that fine-tune or call another company's model generally are not frontier developers unless their own training compute, counted with fine-tuning, crosses the threshold (B&P 22757.11(h), (i)); framework duties apply only to large frontier developers with affiliates' annual gross revenue over $500M (22757.11(j)); 'deploy' excludes making a model available to a third party primarily to develop or evaluate it (22757.11(e)(2)); 'catastrophic risk' excludes information publicly available elsewhere in substantially similar form, lawful federal government activity, and harm from combining the model with other software where the model did not materially contribute (22757.11(c)(2)).
key_definitions: 'frontier model' = a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting the original run plus later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other material modifications (B&P 22757.11(i)); 'foundation model' = an AI model trained on a broad data set, designed for generality of output, and adaptable to a wide range of tasks (22757.11(f)); 'frontier developer' = a person who has trained or initiated training of a frontier model (22757.11(h)); 'large frontier developer' = a frontier developer whose revenue with affiliates exceeded $500M in the preceding calendar year (22757.11(j)); 'catastrophic risk' = foreseeable and material risk that a frontier model materially contributes to death or serious injury of more than 50 people or over $1B in property damage from one incident via CBRN weapon assistance, autonomous cyberattack or crime, or evading control (22757.11(c)); 'critical safety incident' = unauthorized access to model weights causing death or injury, harm from a catastrophic risk, loss of control causing death or injury, or deceptive subversion of developer controls (22757.11(d))
key_questions: Did your company itself train (or start training) a foundation model using more than 10^26 operations, including fine-tuning compute?; Or do you only fine-tune or call a model trained by another company?; Were your company's and affiliates' gross revenues over $500M last calendar year?; Do you make the model available to third parties in California?
obligations: Large frontier developers must write, follow, and publish a frontier AI framework on catastrophic-risk management. Frontier developers must publish a transparency report when deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model and report critical safety incidents to Cal OES within 15 days (24 hours to an appropriate authority if imminent risk of death or serious injury). Whistleblower protections for employees. Large frontier developers must also send Cal OES summaries of any assessment of catastrophic risk from internal use of their frontier models every three months or on another reasonable written schedule (22757.12(d)), and keep unredacted information for five years when they redact published documents (22757.12(f)).
enforcement: Civil penalty up to $1,000,000 per violation against large frontier developers, AG only.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 138, Stats. 2025; approved by Governor 2025-09-29 (also gov.ca.gov 9/29/2025 release). Edge case: health relevance only indirect (health AI vendors building on frontier models are generally not covered). Removed training_data tag; the act has no training-data disclosure duty.

title: No Robo Bosses Act (2025 version; employment ADS)
triggers: Would have applied to employers using automated decision systems on workers.
example_tools: AI productivity or performance monitoring of nurses or call-center staff; automated discipline or deactivation system for gig or contract clinicians; AI scheduling tool that sets quotas or assigns work; AI scoring of employee performance from customer ratings; resume or applicant screening tool
exclusions: Not law (vetoed 2025-10-13); signal only. If it had been signed: employment-only (workers, including independent contractors); the pre-use notice duty excluded hiring decisions, which had a separate applicant notice (Lab. Code 1522(a), (d)); the part would not have applied to parties covered by a collective bargaining agreement that explicitly waives it and protects against algorithmic management (1538); an employer complying with federal-government contractual or regulatory requirements was not barred from doing so (1539); employers complying with substantially similar notice duties under other state law were deemed compliant, except CPPA ADMT rules still applied to CCPA businesses (1536-1537). Superseded in part by SB 947 (2026).
key_definitions: 'automated decision system' = computational process from machine learning, statistical modeling, data analytics, or AI that issues simplified output (score, classification, recommendation) used to assist or replace human discretionary decisionmaking and materially impacts natural persons; excludes spam filters, firewalls, antivirus, identity and access tools, calculators, databases, datasets (Lab. Code 1520(c)); 'employer' = anyone who directly or indirectly employs or controls wages, hours, working conditions or terms for any worker, including public employers and labor contractors (1520(e)); 'worker' = any employee or independent contractor providing service to or through a business or government entity (1520(i)); 'employment-related decision' = decision that materially affects wages, benefits, hours, schedule, evaluation, hiring, discipline, promotion, termination, job tasks, assignment, training access, productivity requirements, or workplace health and safety (1520(f)); 'quota' (1520(h))
key_questions: Is the tool used on employees or contractors (not patients)?; Does it influence discipline, termination, deactivation, scheduling, pay, or productivity quotas?; Does a human review ADS output and other evidence before a discipline, termination, or deactivation decision?; Have you given workers advance written notice and a post-decision notice?; Is the workforce covered by a collective bargaining agreement that waives these rules?
obligations: Would have required advance written notice of workplace ADS use, barred sole reliance on an ADS for discipline, termination, or deactivation, and required human review when relying primarily on ADS output.
enforcement: Not applicable.
notes: Veto 2025-10-13 confirmed in gov.ca.gov 10.13.25 legislative update (veto list) and DD history (veto sustained 2026-03-02). Enrolled text via Digital Democracy (Tier 2). Narrow employment relevance; included as signal.

title: Mental health professionals: artificial intelligence
triggers: Would have applied to entities providing psychotherapy services using AI.
example_tools: AI therapy chatbot marketed as a therapist or counselor; AI scribe that records and transcribes therapy sessions; AI intake triage or mental-health screening tool; AI that generates progress notes or treatment plans for a therapy practice; emotion-detection tool used in a psychotherapy visit
exclusions: Not law (vetoed 2026-09-30); signal only. If it had been signed: excluded religious counseling, peer support, public self-help and educational materials that do not purport to offer psychotherapy, AI used solely for training or simulation, and qualifying academic or nonprofit research (B&P 4989.87); 'psychotherapy services' excluded religious counseling and peer support, and 'psychotherapeutic communication' excluded general wellness education aimed at overall well-being rather than a specific disorder (4989.82(g)(2), (h)); allowed without licensed review: recommending the person discuss their needs with a licensed professional, administering and scoring a standardized screening questionnaire and forwarding it to a licensed professional without using it to assess, and scheduling, reminders, or logistics (4989.84(e)); a licensed professional was not disciplined for violations caused solely by tool features required by their employer (4989.83(c)(2)); AI that directly interacts therapeutically was allowed only if FDA approved or cleared for that use and HIPAA-compliant (4989.84(b)(2)).
key_definitions: 'psychotherapy services' = services provided to diagnose or treat an individual's mental health or substance use disorder; excludes religious counseling and peer support (B&P 4989.82(h)); 'psychotherapeutic communication' = any verbal, nonverbal, or written interaction in a clinical or professional setting conducted to diagnose or treat a mental health or substance use disorder or concern (4989.82(g)); 'administrative support' = scheduling, reminders, billing and claims processing, and general logistics communications without therapeutic advice (4989.82(a)); 'supplementary support' = non-therapeutic tasks such as preparing records and progress notes, data analysis reviewed by a licensed professional, organizing referrals, and AI tools for documentation or workflow where the licensed professional keeps responsibility for clinical decisions and communications (4989.82(j)); 'triage or screening' = assessing health concerns and symptoms to decide urgency, clinical nature, or level of need for psychotherapy (4989.82(k)); 'consent' = a clear, explicit, revocable, documented affirmative act, not a general terms-of-use acceptance (4989.82(d)); 'licensed professional' = the listed licensed or supervised mental health and nursing professionals (4989.82(e)); 'companion chatbot' per B&P 22601 (4989.82(c))
key_questions: Does the tool record or transcribe psychotherapy sessions, triage, or screening, and is verbal or written informed consent obtained and documented?; Does the AI make therapeutic decisions, detect emotions, generate diagnoses, recommendations, or treatment plans, or talk therapeutically with clients, and is a licensed professional reviewing and approving?; Is it FDA-cleared for that use and HIPAA-compliant?; Is a companion chatbot being advertised or offered as therapy or a therapist?; Is it only administrative or documentation support under a licensed professional's responsibility?; Is it religious counseling, peer support, or public self-help content?
obligations: Would have limited AI in psychotherapy services to administrative or supplementary support; required that the client be informed (verbally or in writing) that AI is used and for what purpose, and consent, before AI records or transcribes psychotherapeutic communications, sessions, or triage or screening; barred AI from making therapeutic decisions, generating therapeutic recommendations, assessments, diagnoses, or treatment plans, detecting emotions or mental states, performing triage or screening, or directly engaging in psychotherapeutic communication without licensed-professional review and approval (direct interaction allowed only for tools FDA-approved or cleared for that use and HIPAA-compliant); barred advertising or offering psychotherapy through companion chatbots; required CMIA compliance for AI use in therapy records and barred sharing, selling, storing, or training on therapy data inconsistent with law.
enforcement: Not applicable.
notes: Veto 2026-09-30 confirmed in gov.ca.gov 9.30.2026 legislative update (veto list) and DD history; the Inside Privacy "signed" listing is wrong. Enrolled text read via Digital Democracy (Tier 2). Veto message not read.

title: CCPA deletion rights expansion
triggers: A CCPA business holds personal information collected from or about consumers, including from third parties.
example_tools: data broker or people-search style health marketing database held by a CCPA business; consumer health app that enriches user profiles with third-party data; digital health company's identity-resolution or lead-enrichment pipeline; AI model training dataset built from purchased consumer data; online-only wellness subscription service handling deletion requests
exclusions: Amends deletion rights only for CCPA 'businesses' (for-profit; revenue above $26,625,000, 100,000+ consumers or households, or 50%+ of revenue from selling/sharing; Civ. Code 1798.140(d)). Medical information governed by the CMIA and PHI held by HIPAA covered entities and business associates remain outside the CCPA (1798.145(c)). Deletion is not required where retention is reasonably necessary to complete the transaction, provide a requested good or service, ensure security and integrity, debug, exercise free speech or other legal rights, comply with CalECPA, support qualifying research with informed consent, support compatible internal uses, or comply with a legal obligation (1798.105(d)). A business that got data from a non-consumer source is deemed compliant if it keeps a record of the deletion request and the minimum data necessary to keep the information deleted (1798.105(c)(2)). Service providers and contractors need not honor requests sent directly to them for data held in that role (1798.105(c)(4)).
key_definitions: deletion right now covers 'any personal information about the consumer which the business has collected from or about the consumer' (Civ. Code 1798.105(a)); 'business' = see CA-CCPA thresholds (1798.140(d)); 'consumer' = California resident natural person (1798.140(i)); online-only businesses with a direct consumer relationship need provide only an email address and an online request method; businesses with websites must accept requests there (1798.130(a)(1)); response within 45 days, extendable once by 45 days (1798.130(a)(2))
key_questions: Is the company a CCPA business over the thresholds?; Does it hold personal information about consumers that it got from third parties, data brokers, or partners?; Is that data CMIA medical information or HIPAA PHI (exempt) or other consumer data (covered)?; Is the business online-only with a direct relationship to consumers (email plus online method suffices)?; Can you propagate deletion to service providers, contractors, and third parties it was sold or shared with?
obligations: Honor deletion requests for personal information collected "from or about" the consumer, including data obtained from third parties (subject to existing retention exceptions); online-only businesses with a direct consumer relationship must provide an email address and an online request method, and businesses with websites must accept requests through them.
enforcement: CPPA and AG.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 482, Stats. 2026; approved by Governor 2026-09-27. Default effective 2027-01-01. Edge: CCPA amendment with indirect health relevance; CMIA/HIPAA exemptions still apply.

title: California AI Transparency Act
effective_date_notes: As enacted, operative 2026-01-01 (22757.6); AB 853 (2025) moved the chapter operative date to 2026-08-02. SB 1000 (urgency, 2026-09-30) rewrote 22757.1-22757.5.
trigger_rule: ca_users AND generates_media AND (trains_genai_model OR NOT third_party_model)
triggers: A covered provider creates or produces a generative AI system publicly accessible in California that can create or alter image, video, or audio content. The original 1,000,000-monthly-user threshold was removed by SB 1000 (2026).
example_tools: AI medical image generator (synthetic X-rays, dermatology images); AI video avatar for patient education; AI voice generator or text-to-speech for health content; generative tool that edits or enhances clinical photos; publicly accessible image or video generation app
exclusions: Does not apply to a product, service, website, or app that provides exclusively non-user-generated video games (B&P 22757.5(a), as amended by SB 1000); before 2029-01-01, does not apply to a GenAI system designed to primarily function as assistive technology (22757.5(b)); latent disclosure and verification duties cover image, video, and audio content, not text-only output, and exclude content changed only by minor modification (brightness, contrast, color, sharpening, resizing, cropping, format conversion, denoising) (22757.2(a), 22757.3(a), 22757.1(l)); latent disclosures required only to the extent technically feasible (22757.3(a)); covered providers need not monitor licensees (22757.3(b)(5)).
key_definitions: 'covered provider' = a person that creates, codes, or otherwise produces a generative AI system publicly accessible within California (B&P 22757.1(e), as amended by SB 1000; the original 1,000,000 monthly user threshold was removed); 'GenAI system' = AI that can generate derived synthetic content, including text, images, video, and audio, emulating its training data (22757.1(g)); 'minor modification' = brightness/contrast/color changes, sharpening, saturating, resizing, scaling, cropping, format conversion, audio denoising (22757.1(l)); 'assistive technology' = item, equipment, or product system used to increase, maintain, or improve functional capabilities of people with disabilities (22757.1(b))
key_questions: Does your generative AI system create or alter images, video, or audio (vs. text only)?; Is it publicly accessible in California?; Did you create, code, or produce it (vs. license it from another provider)?; Do you license your system to third parties who might strip disclosures?; Is it designed primarily as assistive technology for people with disabilities?
obligations: Covered providers must embed latent provenance disclosures in AI-generated image, video, and audio content, offer a free public detection (now "disclosure verification") tool, and manage licensees whose modified systems drop disclosures. The original duty to offer users an optional manifest disclosure was removed by SB 1000 (2026).
enforcement: Civil penalty $5,000 per violation per day, recoverable by the AG, city attorneys, or county counsel, plus attorney's fees.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 291, Stats. 2024; approved by Governor 2024-09-19. Edge case: touches health only indirectly. Obligations describe current law as amended by AB 853 and SB 1000.

title: No Robo Bosses Act (employment automated decision systems)
triggers: An employer (including public employers and labor contractors) uses an automated decision system for disciplinary or termination decisions about workers in California, including health-care employers.
example_tools: AI productivity monitoring of nurses or call-center staff used for discipline; algorithmic scheduling or attendance scoring that triggers write-ups; AI performance-scoring tool for home health aides; automated termination recommendations for hospital staff
exclusions: Does not apply to parties covered by a collective bargaining agreement that explicitly waives the part in clear terms and provides for wages, working conditions, and protection from algorithmic management (Lab. Code 1526.5); does not apply to ADS use required by or reasonably necessary to comply with federal law or binding federal contracts on aircraft development or national security, military, space, or defense products (1526.6); 'automated decision system' excludes spam filters, firewalls, antivirus, identity and access management tools, calculators, databases, datasets, or other data compilations (1520(c)); core limits apply to disciplinary and termination decisions, not hiring; notice-equivalence provision does not apply to quotas or other automated standards applied to working conditions (1526.3).
key_definitions: 'automated decision system' = computational process from ML, statistical modeling, data analytics, or AI issuing simplified output (score, classification, recommendation) used to assist or replace human discretionary decisionmaking that materially impacts natural persons; excludes spam filters, firewalls, antivirus, identity/access tools, calculators, databases, datasets (Lab. Code 1520(c)); 'employer' = anyone who directly or indirectly employs or controls wages, hours, or working conditions, including state and local government entities and labor contractors (1520(d)(3)); 'ADS output' = information, predictions, scores, recommendations, decisions, or conclusions generated by an ADS (1520(a)); 'employee data' (1520(d)(4))
key_questions: Is the tool used by an employer (including a public employer or labor contractor) for decisions about California employees?; Is it used for discipline or termination decisions?; Does the employer rely solely or primarily on the tool's output?; Is a human reviewing and corroborating the output with other information?; Are the workers covered by a collective bargaining agreement that expressly waives this law?
obligations: Do not rely solely on an ADS for discipline or termination; if primarily relying on ADS output, have a human corroborate it with other information, and do not use uncorroborated or inaccurate output; give a written post-use notice; on request, describe the employee's data the ADS used; do not use an ADS to infer protected status, violate labor or civil rights law, or predict and punish the exercise of legal rights; no retaliation.
enforcement: Labor Commissioner (citations, temporary relief, civil action) and public prosecutors; civil penalty of $500 per violation; injunctive relief and attorney's fees.
notes: Tier 2 mirror: CalMatters Digital Democracy (chaptered text + bill history). Ch. 859, Stats. 2026; approved by Governor 2026-09-30 (gov.ca.gov 9.30.2026 AI release). Narrow employment tag. Successor to vetoed SB 7 (2025). The 2027-07-01 date is confirmed in the text. Typo fixed: "Wilson-type alert" was the Wiley alert (no longer relied on).
